title: Clinicopathologic Predictors of PSMA-PET Detection, Recurrence Pattern, and Biochemical Outcome Following Salvage Radiotherapy After Radical Prostatectomy
abstract: Purpose Biochemical recurrence (BCR) after radical prostatectomy (RP) presents heterogeneous recurrence patterns and variable outcomes following salvage radiotherapy (sRT). We evaluated clinicopathologic determinants of PSMA-PET/CT detection, anatomical recurrence distribution, and biochemical disease-free survival (bDFS) following PSMA-PET-guided sRT. Methods This retrospective single-institution study included 140 patients with BCR after RP who underwent 68 Ga-PSMA-PET/CT prior to sRT with or without androgen deprivation therapy. PSMA-PET-positive findings were categorized as prostate bed only (PBO) or pelvic nodal involvement with or without the prostate bed (PLNI). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, logistic regression, and Cox proportional hazards models were employed. Results PSMA-PET detected locoregional recurrence in 77/140 patients (55%). On multivariable analysis, PSA at recurrence (OR=2.07; p=0.003) and age (OR=1.07; p=0.016) were the sole independent predictors of PSMA-PET positivity. ROC analysis yielded AUC=0.74 (optimal threshold of 0.58 ng/mL). Among PSMA-positive patients, PBO was associated with a longer time to BCR (tBCR) (37.5 versus 15 months; p=0.006). Seminal vesicle invasion (SVI) and pT-stage predicted PLNI on univariable analysis. Among 124 of 140 evaluable patients (median follow-up 31 months), estimated bDFS at 24, 36, and 60 months was 89.7%, 80.2%, and 54.1%, respectively. SVI (HR=2.39; p=0.031), EPE (HR=2.82; p=0.012), pT-stage (HR=1.64; p=0.021), and pN-stage (HR=1.83; p=0.045) were associated with increased failure on univariable Cox regression, though none retained independent significance. Conclusion PSA burden and age independently predicted PSMA-PET detection. Recurrence patterns reflected disease behavior, as PBO was associated with longer tBCR. Adverse pathologic features were associated with pelvic nodal disease and reduced biochemical control; none remained independently predictive.

title: Deep Learning-Based Anatomical Level Classification of Craniofacial CT Slices: Comparison of CNN Architectures and Ensemble Methods
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) interpretation requires recognition of the anatomical level of each slice. Classification may facilitate preprocessing and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. We developed deep learning models to classify craniofacial CT slices into six anatomical categories. A total of 11,769 images were collected from a multicenter database involving 10 Japanese university hospitals and the public Head-Neck-Radiomics-HN1 dataset. Patients were divided into training (70%) and evaluation (30%) sets. Five CNN architectures were trained from scratch, and hard- and soft-voting ensembles were evaluated. Individual-model accuracy ranged from 94.72% to 96.09%; the hard-voting ensemble achieved 96.46% accuracy (Cohens {kappa} = 0.954). Although performance differed among individual models (Cochrans Q = 99.29, p < 0.001), the ensemble did not significantly outperform EfficientNetV2B1 (McNemars p = 0.163). Errors occurred mainly between adjacent anatomical regions. Deep learning can classify craniofacial CT slices accurately and may support automated dataset organization and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. External validation is needed.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology in Thyroid Diseases: Comparison with Histopathological Findings in Hawassa, Ethiopia
abstract: Introduction Thyroid diseases are major health problems and among the most common endocrine disorders worldwide, including in Ethiopia. They are characterized by alterations in hormone secretion, enlargement of the thyroid gland, or both. Fine needle aspiration cytology is an important initial screening tool, and histopathologic examination is essential for the definitive diagnosis of thyroid disease. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology with histopathology in identifying thyroid diseases. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted at three health facilities in Hawassa City, Ethiopia, involving 304 patients who underwent both thyroid fine needle aspiration cytology and histopathologic examination of the same site between 30 th October 2024 and 29 th October 2025. FNAC results were classified using the Bethesda system, with histopathology as the gold standard. Data were entered into Kobo Toolbox, exported to SPSS version 27, and analyzed using cross-tabulation and chi-square (χ 2 ) tests to determine diagnostic accuracy. Result 304 patient records were included in the study. The fine needle aspiration cytology was determinate/diagnostic in 81.6% of cases. The study revealed the sensitivity and specificity of fine needle aspiration cytology to be 88.2% (CI 77.6-95.1%) and 94.4% (CI 90.6-97.1%), respectively. The false negative and false positive rates in this study were 2.4% and 4.4%, respectively. The positive predictive value was 80.3% (CI 68.7-89.3%), and the negative predictive value was 96.8% (CI 93.8-98.7%). The accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology in differentiating benign from malignant thyroid lesions was 93.1%. Conclusion FNAC demonstrated strong agreement with histopathology and remains a reliable, cost-effective first-line diagnostic tool for thyroid disease, particularly in resource-limited settings. Strengthening sample handling, ultrasound guidance, and adherence to Bethesda criteria may further improve diagnostic precision

title: Neurochemical fingerprinting of the Alzheimers disease continuum using 7 T short-echo-time brain single voxel 1H-MRS.
abstract: IntroductionThis study aimed to characterize the neurochemical profile of Alzheimers disease (AD) continuum stages using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) data for brain metabolites and macromolecules. We used Orthogonal Projection to Latent Structures Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) to classify diagnostic groups and assess feature importance. MethodsOur dataset consisted of 7 T short-echo time 1H-MRS spectra of the posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus of individuals diagnosed with AD (n = 27) or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI, n = 27) and Healthy Controls (HC, n = 31). Classification used 100-round Monte Carlo cross-validation based on metabolite concentrations and macromolecular peak intensities. Variable importance in projection (VIP) was assessed across classification models to identify the most relevant neurochemical features. The resulting metabolite rankings were compared with previous literature to evaluate their biological plausibility. ResultsClassification was strongest for AD versus HC (AUC=0.88) and lower for comparisons involving MCI. Metabolites contributing most strongly to classification included myo-inositol, ascorbate, and choline-containing compounds, consistent with previous studies on AD-related neurochemical alterations. In addition, specific macromolecular components were identified as relevant features, suggesting a potential contribution of MM signals to the characterization of AD-related neurochemistry. DiscussionThese findings support the use of short-echo-time 1H-MRS as a complementary tool for characterizing neurochemical changes in the AD continuum, with potential applications in disease characterization and monitoring, warranting validation in larger cohorts.

title: Preclinical Evaluation of [ 18 F]Itareparib, a brain penetrant PARP1-selective radioligand, in Glioma Rat Model and Nonhuman Primate
abstract: ABSTRACT Rationale Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP1) is a central mediator of DNA damage response and is upregulated in glioma, supporting it as a molecular imaging biomarker. However, quantitative PET assessment of PARP1 in infiltrative tumors with a preserved blood-brain barrier remains an unmet need. In this study, we evaluated if [ 18 F]Itareparib, a brain-penetrant, non-trapping, PARP1-selective radioligand with reversible kinetics, could improve brain tumor diagnosis and enable target occupancy studies in neurooncology. Methods [ 18 F]Itareparib was synthesized and evaluated in an orthotopic rat model of BT142 IDH1-mutant gliomas. Dynamic PET scans were performed with or without the administration of the PARP1-selective inhibitor AZD9574. Standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) for tumors were calculated using the contralateral region as reference and compared with distribution volume ratios (DVRs) calculated using kinetic modeling. PARP1-specific binding and tracer stability were assessed using autoradiography, immunofluorescence, biodistribution, and radiometabolite analysis. Brain kinetics of [ 18 F]Itareparib were evaluated in a healthy nonhuman primate (NHP) at baseline and blocking conditions. Results [ 18 F]Itareparib rapidly entered the rat brains and showed 4-fold higher uptake in BT142 tumors than in the contralateral brain. AZD9574 reduced tumor uptake by 77%, supporting the PARP1-specific binding of [ 18 F]Itareparib in the tumors. SUVR (30–60 min) showed the closest agreement with DVR. Autoradiographic tumor-to-reference mean ratio was 7.3, and AZD9574 reduced the tumor-to-reference ratio by 56%. PARP1 immunofluorescence was higher in tumor than the rest of the brain and correlated with autoradiographic results. In rats, the parent fraction of [ 18 F]Itareparib exceeded 99% in brain through 60 min post tracer injection ( p.i. ) and was approximately 88% in plasma at 60 min p.i. In the NHP, [ 18 F]Itareparib showed rapid brain uptake, and V T decreased by 21 ± 6 % after blocking with AZD9574. Conclusion [ 18 F]Itareparib showed brain penetration, high in vivo metabolic stability, reversible binding kinetics, and PARP1-specific tumor uptake. These findings support further development of [ 18 F]Itareparib for the quantitative PET imaging of PARP1 in brain tumors.

title: Aberrant cortical reorganization and astrogliosis underlie memory deficit post-traumatic brain injury: a longitudinal multiscale multimodal study
abstract: Integrating high-dimensional neuroimaging data across spatial scales remains a fundamental bottleneck in quantitative neuroscience. Here, we apply emerging analytical techniques including functional connectome gradient mapping and 3D segmentation of whole-brain cellular resolution microscopy data in a mouse model of traumatic brain injury. At the macroscale, longitudinal functional MRI revealed a transition from frontal hyperconnectivity to hippocampal hypoconnectivity and unimodal-transmodal gradient contraction indicating network dedifferentiation. At the cellular scale, deep-learning based segmentation of whole-brain light-sheet fluorescence microscopy volumes quantified regional astrogliosis, neuronal hyperactivity, and single-axon loss undetected by standard diffusion MRI. Multiscale multimodal data integration not only identified quantitative biomarkers predictive of memory performance post-injury but also enabled validation of in vivo modalities against more sensitive ex vivo histology. This study demonstrates a framework for probing complex multi-network cognitive functions and neurological disorders of network dysfunction.

title: TiSAM: fusing spatial and histopathology foundation models for whole-slide image segmentation
abstract: Semantic segmentation of whole-slide images (WSIs) quantifies tissue composition and architecture, but existing models require extensive annotation and lose accuracy as the number of tissue classes increases or on heterogeneous, cross-scanner datasets. Here, we present the Tissue Segment Anything Model (TiSAM), which fuses SAM3 spatial features with UNI2-h pathology features within a multi-scale decoder. Because public benchmarks contain few tissue classes, we release MegaMouse, comprising 36,833 annotations of 52 tissue classes from 12 mouse organs, and an 11-class human pancreas dataset. TiSAM achieved the highest overall performance across four public datasets compared to existing convolutional neural network and vision transformer models, maintained high accuracy on MegaMouse, and maintained high accuracy in the human pancreas dataset when trained on as few as 5 annotated WSIs where previous integrations of SAM with pathology foundation models did not. TiSAM segmentations were also more consistent across eight slide scanners compared to other models. These results establish TiSAM as a general and highly adaptable framework for tissue segmentation, enabling studies containing many tissue classes, limited annotations, or images from multiple scanners.

title: Claims-based reconstruction of the pancreatic cancer care pathway links centralization of care to survival
abstract: Background The organization of pancreatic cancer care may be associated with survival. Using health administrative claims data, we reconstructed the pathway from diagnosis to first-line therapy and examined associations of multidisciplinary team review and treatment at specialized centers with overall survival. Methods Longitudinal historical cohort study using anonymized health administrative claims data from six Czech health insurance funds, covering approximately 17% of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer nationally between 2018 and 2020. Adults with an incident ICD-10 C25 record confirmed by imaging and histopathology were followed from the index date (the date of the first qualifying imaging or histopathological examination) until death, censoring, or 31 December 2021. Overall survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier methods and Cox regression adjusted for age and first-line therapy type. Results Of 1,255 patients, 920 (73.3%) received first-line therapy and 266 (21.2%) died untreated. Among treated patients, 436 (47.4%) underwent multidisciplinary team review, 335 (36.4%) underwent surgery, and 667 (72.5%) were treated at a complex oncological center. Surgery was associated with longer overall survival than chemotherapy (age-adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.32, P < 0.001). Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer overall survival (adjusted HR 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64–0.92, P = 0.004; crude median 532 versus 394 days). Multidisciplinary team review was not significantly associated with overall survival (adjusted HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73–1.01, P = 0.073). Conclusions Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer survival, while fewer than half of patients had a recorded multidisciplinary team review. How care is organized, not only which therapy is delivered, is associated with outcome. The observational design and absence of key clinical covariates limit causal interpretation.

title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
abstract: Background: Ultra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimaging, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. Methods: We systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort(N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. Results: MIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader distinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. Conclusions: Structural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

title: Clinical referral text overrides MRI evidence in multimodal large language models: glioma versus brain abscess
abstract: ObjectivesTo determine how strongly clinical referral text, rather than image content, drives the decisions of multimodal large language models (LLMs) differentiating glioma from brain abscess on MRI. Materials and methodsThis retrospective single-center study included 60 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI examinations (30 gliomas, 30 abscesses; reference-standard diagnosis). One axial slice per case was paired with five referral texts (explicitly inflammatory to explicitly tumor-suggestive) under three prompt instructions and submitted 20 times each to GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Qwen 3.6 (72,000 answers). The primary outcome was the text-driven span (difference in tumor-call frequency between explicit inflammatory and explicit tumor text). Two blinded radiologists classified the images without text; sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were compared descriptively. ResultsPatients (29 women) had a mean age of 55.8 {+/-} 16.4 years. With neutral text, models answered tumor in 45-67% of queries (specificity, 0.38-0.78), versus 52% and 60% for radiologists (specificity, 0.77 and 0.63). The text-driven span was 0.79-1.00 (p < 0.001 for all models), whereas confirmed gliomas and abscesses differed by only 0.01-0.10 in three models and 0.25 in Gemini 3.5 Flash. Subtle wording produced at least 83% of the span in three models. An instruction to ignore the text reduced the span to 0.48-0.70 in three models and to 0.04 in Gemini 3.5 Flash, partly through reversion to a tumor default. Model accuracy was 0.52-0.73 versus 0.78 and 0.73 for radiologists. ConclusionMultimodal LLMs deferred to referral text over imaging evidence in differentiating glioma from brain abscess, and prompt instructions did not reliably correct this. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSMultimodal large language models receive images together with clinical referral text, but how strongly the text rather than the image determines their diagnosis is unknown. FindingsChanging only the referral text largely reversed the glioma-versus-abscess decision for identical MRI images in four models; instructions to ignore the text reduced this inconsistently. Clinical relevanceBefore clinical use, multimodal large language models require model- and task-specific testing of their susceptibility to referral text, because instructing them to prioritize the image is not a dependable safeguard against text-driven misdiagnosis.

title: Beyond Segmentation Accuracy: Evaluating Biological Fidelity in Spatial Pathology
abstract: Multiplex immunofluorescence (MxIF) resolves cellular identity, state, and spatial organization within tumor tissue, enabling higher-order representations of cancer ecosystems including immune infiltration, multicellular neighborhoods, and tissue niches. Yet these analyses depend on a deceptively simple first step: accurately identifying individual cells. Segmentation errors can alter marker quantification, cellular phenotypes, cell–cell relationships, and ultimately the spatial organization inferred from an image. Consequently, improvements in conventional segmentation benchmarks matter biologically only if they propagate to more faithful representations of the tumor microenvironment. We test this relationship directly using an expert-curated benchmark of 31,924 expert-reviewed cells on three slides under a leave-slide-out protocol. We compare a domain-specific self-supervised encoder, adapted to multiplex tissue imaging, with supervised, microscopy-specific, prompted generalist, and general-purpose vision models, and pass every method’s predicted cells through an identical downstream pipeline. We evaluate fidelity across four levels: cell segmentation, phenotype assignment, spatial neighborhood structure, and tissue organization, comprising niches and tumor–immune interactions. The resulting hierarchy reveals that these levels do not improve in lockstep. Cellular phenotype assignment is comparatively robust to segmentation differences, whereas missed cells increasingly disrupt neighborhood structure and tumor–immune interactions. As a stringent spatial-interaction test, tumor–CD8 + contact recovery is poorly predicted by conventional segmentation quality (Panoptic Quality: ρ = 0.18), while errors specifically at tumor–immune interfaces are strongly associated with contact fidelity ( ρ = −0.80). Methods with nearly identical segmentation accuracy can therefore produce substantially different biological representations. These results argue that cell segmentation for spatial pathology should be evaluated not only by boundary and instance accuracy, but also by preservation of the biological relationships that downstream analyses are intended to measure.

abstract: The m-Bonacci weighted sequence space [Formula] is introduced for m [≥]2, 1[≤]p < {infty}, and > 0. title: Individual-level Structural Neuroimaging Biomarkers across the Psychosis Spectrum
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Hypothesis Although psychotic disorders are characterized by widespread cortical thinning, translating these findings into individualized biomarkers remains challenging. Regional Vulnerability Index (RVI) and Neuroscore are candidate individual-level biomarkers that quantify the similarity between an individual’s structural brain pattern and generic psychosis-associated alterations. This study investigated cortical thickness (CT)-based RVI and Neuroscore, along with mean CT deviation from healthy individuals, across the psychosis spectrum. Study Design Using structural 3T MRI data from 289 participants (clinical high risk for psychosis [CHR], n=39; first episode psychosis [FEP], n=44, chronic psychosis [CP], n=86; healthy controls [HC], n=120), RVI, Neuroscore, and mean CT deviation (z) scores were computed from region-wise CT measures quantified using FreeSurfer v7.2. Group differences and associations with symptoms were evaluated. Study Results RVI and Neuroscore were significantly higher, and mean CT z-scores lower, in FEP and CP compared with CHR and HC, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (|Cohen’s d| = 0.55–1.15). No differences were observed between FEP and CP or CHR and HC. Indices were not associated with psychosis-spectrum symptom severity in the CHR, FEP, or CP groups. RVI ( r = −0.561, p < .001) and Neuroscore ( r = −0.997, p < .001) were strongly negatively correlated with the mean CT z-score. Conclusions CT-based RVI and Neuroscore appear to index established disease status but not risk status, while showing substantial overlap with mean CT deviation. These findings highlight the need to further refine these biomarkers through data-driven and multimodal approaches to improve their utility for risk and prognostic prediction.

title: Anatomically Programmable and Optically Tunable 3D-Bioprinted Tumor-Mimicking Phantoms for Quantitative Nanofluorophore Benchmarking
abstract: Surgical resection remains a primary treatment for solid tumors, with fluorescence-guided surgery offering improved intraoperative visualization and precision. However, conventional murine models provide limited control over anatomical and optical variables critical to evaluating fluorescent imaging agents. Here, we developed 3D-bioprinted, anatomically tailored and optically tunable tumor-mimicking phantoms (TMPs) as a reproducible platform for quantitative nanofluorophore evaluation under tissue-relevant surgical conditions. These TMPs recreate subcutaneous, epithelial, and intraperitoneal tumor presentations while enabling controlled variation of lesion geometry, spatial distribution, tissue pigmentation, cellular composition, and nanofluorophore concentration. Semiconducting polymer nanofluorophores (SPNs) with distinct emission profiles were incorporated as model imaging agents and evaluated using an in vivo imaging system (IVIS). The engineered phantoms enabled quantitative assessment of wavelength-dependent fluorescence, lesion visualization and delineation across diverse geometries and tissue backgrounds, multiplexed imaging of spatially distinct lesions, and simulation of fluorescence-guided tumor resection. Constructs incorporating GFP-expressing cancer cells further demonstrated simultaneous visualization of cellular and nanoprobe-derived fluorescence. Collectively, these findings establish anatomically programmable TMPs as a versatile, reproducible framework for benchmarking fluorescent imaging agents, systematically interrogating anatomical and optical determinants of imaging performance, and advancing fluorescence-guided surgical strategies before in vivo evaluation and clinical translation.

title: Discrepancies in Interpretation of Japanese Radiology Report Expressions Between Radiologists and Referring Physicians
abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate discrepancies between radiologists and referring physicians in the interpretation of diagnostic probabilities conveyed by common Japanese expressions used in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsFifteen expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities in radiology reports were selected by five attending radiologists. An anonymous online survey was distributed to 26 radiologists and 33 referring physicians at a single institution. Participants assigned a diagnostic probability (from 0% to 100% in 10% increments) to each expression. Differences in median probabilities between radiologists and referring physicians were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Variability in interpretation was assessed using interquartile range (IQR), with IQR [≥] 30% defined as substantial variability. ResultsAll radiologists (26/26) and 97% of referring physicians (32/33) completed the survey. Seven of the 15 expressions showed statistically significant differences in interpretation between radiologists and referring physicians: "c/w" (80% vs. 60%; p = 0.031), the Japanese equivalents of "present" (100% vs. 100%; p = 0.024), "suspect of" (80% vs. 70%; p = 0.007), "possibly" (50% vs. 70%; p < 0.001), "unlikely" (10% vs. 10%; p = 0.022), "cannot be ruled out" (25% vs. 40%; p < 0.001), and "not inconsistent with" (80% vs. 90%; p = 0.008). Substantial variability in interpretation (IQR [≥] 30%) was observed for four expressions: "cannot be ruled out" (IQR, 10%-40%), "s/o" (IQR, 60%-90%), "c/w" (IQR, 50%-90%), and "not inconsistent with" (IQR, 70%-100%). ConclusionThis study revealed that nearly half of the Japanese expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities were interpreted differently by radiologists and referring physicians. These discrepancies highlight the need for a standardized lexicon to improve clarity and consistency in radiology reporting. Compliance with Reporting GuidelinesThis study was conducted in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies.

title: Prevalence and Clinical Correlates of Coronary Perivascular Inflammation in an Asymptomatic Adult Primary Prevention Population: An Assessment of the CT-Derived Fat Attenuation Index Score (FAI-Score)
abstract: Background Coronary perivascular fat attenuation index score (FAI-Score) on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) quantifies vascular inflammation and predicts cardiac mortality in symptomatic cohorts. However, its prevalence, anatomical distribution, and clinical correlates in asymptomatic primary prevention populations remain uncharacterized. Methods In an IRB-approved prospective study across two clinical sites, 84 consecutive asymptomatic adults (mean age 53.7 ± 8.6 years; 63.1% men) with no prior coronary artery disease underwent screening CCTA and comprehensive clinical, metabolic, and biomarker profiling. AI-standardized FAI-Score was quantified across three epicardial vessels (LAD, LCx, RCA). High and very high perivascular inflammation were pre-specified as any vessel ≥75th and ≥90th percentiles, respectively. Luminal stenosis and plaque were graded using CAD-RADS 2.0. Results Elevated FAI-Score (≥75th percentile) was present in 42.9% of participants (36/84; 95% CI 32.8% - 53.5%), with 17.9% (15/84; 95% CI 11.1% - 27.4%) exhibiting very high inflammation (≥90th percentile). Multi-vessel inflammation was identified in 17.9% (15/84), with the RCA most frequently involved (≥90th percentile in 13.1%). Standard circulating biomarkers, including ApoB, non-HDL-C, HbA1c, and PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk showed no association with binary inflammation. Systemic hs-CRP (median 0.8 mg/L) exhibited an inverse correlation with maximum vessel FAI-Score (Spearman ρ=−0.27, p=0.014). Men demonstrated higher rates of elevated FAI-Score than women (52.8% vs. 25.8%, p=0.016; ≥90th percentile: 26.4% vs. 3.2%, p=0.007). Strikingly, 46.2% (30/65) of participants with normal luminal anatomy (CAD-RADS 0) and 47.2% (25/53) with zero plaque burden harbored elevated FAI-Score; all 15 individuals with very high FAI-Score had CAD-RADS 0 (Fisher’s exact p=0.018). Body mass index was the sole secondary correlate surviving false discovery rate correction (AUC = 0.71, p=0.001, all-test FDR q=0.028). Regularized multivariable models showed modest out-of-sample discrimination for FAI-Score elevation (cross-validated AUC = 0.71). Conclusions Coronary perivascular inflammation is common among asymptomatic adults and frequently uncouples from structural plaque and luminal stenosis. Routine circulating biomarkers and clinical risk calculators fail to identify inflamed vessels, highlighting FAI-Score as an independent dimension of primary cardiovascular risk assessment.

title: Development of a deep learning model for glomerulus detection and segmentation in kidney histopathology images
abstract: Background: Estimation of nephron number, an indicator of renal reserve, requires quantitative assessment of glomerular number and size in kidney biopsy specimens. We aimed to develop an automated system for quantitative measurement of glomerular areas from clinical kidney biopsy images, across diverse kidney diseases. Methods: We developed a two-stage deep learning system combining Faster R-CNN for glomerular detection in whole-slide images (WSIs) and DeepLabV3+ for segmentation. Of 114 kidney biopsies (228 WSIs), 104 were used for model development and 10 for independent final evaluation. Agreement was assessed using the F1-score for detection, the Dice coefficient for segmentation, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for glomerular area measurement. Analysis was performed at 40× total magnification (2.331 μm/pixel) and validated against 400× images. Results: In the independent evaluation set, the artificial intelligence (AI) model achieved a mean F1-score of 0.851 for detection, compared with 0.888 among experts. For segmentation, the Dice coefficient was 0.959 ± 0.011 and the per-pair ICC (2,1) for area measurement was 0.989 ± 0.009; both were comparable to inter-expert agreement. Bland–Altman analysis showed a mean bias of −344 μm 2 (95% limits of agreement, −1904 to 1216 μm 2 ) between 40× and 400× measurements. Conclusion: The two-stage model achieved glomerular segmentation and area measurement comparable to expert agreement in independent clinical data, with detection performance approaching inter-expert agreement, and provided reliable measurements at low magnification. This automated approach may facilitate large-scale quantitative kidney pathology and nephron number estimation from clinical kidney biopsies.

title: Leapfrogging cancer diagnostics with AI: a mixed-methods assessment of implementation determinants in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Introduction Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diagnostic pathology capacity is constrained. AI applied to routine histopathology could strengthen diagnostic capacity and offer leapfrogging potential by embedding AI into diagnostic systems as they are built up. However, without empirically identifying implementation determinants in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings, AI solutions risk being poorly aligned with local constraints, limiting impact or exacerbating existing disparities. Methods We conducted an exploratory mixed-methods pilot study across three phases: 1) a structured survey characterising the diagnostic and technical landscape and AI priorities; 2) focus group discussions (FGDs) to inductively identify implementation determinants and 3) a second survey quantifying FGD-derived themes. Twelve physicians were purposively recruited (10 from LMIC, 2 from high-income countries for reference) and findings integrated through narrative triangulation. Results There was substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic and AI infrastructure that did not track consistently with country income classification. H&E staining was universally available, immunohistochemistry capacity was rudimentary at 7 of 10 sites and molecular testing absent or minimal at 6 of 10 sites. Whole-slide-imaging scanners were available at 8 of 10 sites, while graphical processing units, required for efficient AI inference, were available at only 4 of 10 sites. The participants would prioritise use of AI for cancer screening, cancer diagnosis, and biomarker prediction from H&E slides. Six implementation determinants were identified: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration. Financial constraints emerged as the dominant barrier across all determinants, and collaboration as an important enabling mechanism. Conclusion AI implementation readiness in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings is highly heterogeneous and cannot be inferred from income classification, underscoring the need for institution-level assessment. Realising the leapfrogging potential of AI in this context requires coordinated progress across all determinants, with sustainable financing, and collaboration enabling the remaining determinants. Key messages What is already known on this topic? Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in LMICs, where diagnostic capacity and molecular testing capabilities are severely constrained. AI could alleviate gaps, yet evidence on implementation determinants for integrating AI into cancer diagnostics in these settings remains limited. What this study adds? AI implementation readiness varies substantially within LMIC settings and does not track with country income classification. Readiness is shaped by six implementation determinants: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration, with financial constraints as the dominant cross-cutting barrier. How this study might affect research, practice or policy? These findings support institution-level feasibility assessment over income-classification proxies and highlight the need for sustainable financing and collaboration as foundational prerequisites for AI implementation in cancer diagnostics in LMICs.

title: Beyond Kidney Volume: 3D Mapping of Parenchymal, Cortical and Medullary Thickness with Disease, Anthropometry and Kidney Adiposity
abstract: Introduction Kidney volume is associated with renal function, but conventional whole-organ measurements may miss regional changes in kidney substructures. We used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to test whether kidney substructure volumes and three-dimensional (3D) thickness phenotypes are associated with disease, adiposity, and incident outcomes. Methods Automated abdominal MRI segmentations from 70,270 UK Biobank participants were used to quantify left and right kidney cortex, medulla, and parenchyma volumes and mesh-based thickness maps. Mass univariate regression generated statistical parametric maps linking regional thickness to anthropometric traits and disease (CKD, type-2 diabetes [T2D], hypertension). Bidirectional causal mediation analyses were performed using kidney substructure volumetric, thickness PCs and kidney adiposity. Longitudinal changes were assessed in 2,610 participants with repeat imaging. Cox proportional hazards models tested the associations between kidney volumes and principal component (PC) scores of thickness and incident CKD, T2D, hypertension, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and mortality. Results CKD was associated with thinning of the parenchyma and most pronounced in the medulla (87.7% left, 72.8% right), whereas associations in the cortex were mixed. In contrast, T2D and hypertension were predominantly associated with increased thickness, most extensively in the cortex (T2D: 84.39% left, 96.35% right; hypertension: 94.8% left, 99.9% right). Age-disease interactions were associated with reduced thickness across all conditions. Smaller medulla volume and lower cortical thickness mediated the association between CKD and renal sinus fat. Kidney substructure volume was inversely associated with incident CKD across all substructures and both kidney sides (p<0.05), but positively associated with incident hypertension and mortality (p<0.05). Thickness PC scores also predicted outcomes independently of volume, with PC3 in the left cortex (HR 0.91 [0.84– 0.98]), reflecting inferior pole/hilar thickness, associated with incident CKD. Conclusions MRI-derived kidney substructure volumes and 3D thickness maps provide complementary, spatially-resolved markers of kidney morphology, that are mechanistically linked to renal adiposity and future disease risk. Translational Statement / Lay Summary This study used MRI scans from the UK Biobank to examine kidney structure in much greater detail than is possible with standard measurements of kidney size or volume. Instead of treating the kidney as a single organ, we measured tissue thickness at thousands of locations across its three main layers: the cortex (outer layer), medulla (inner layer), and parenchyma (the main functional tissue). Thinning of these regions can indicate tissue loss, while thickening may reflect swelling or other structural changes. We found that ageing, body composition, fat around and within the kidney, and conditions such as chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension were each associated with distinct patterns of structural change thickening across different parts of the kidney. These detailed 3D thickness maps reveal changes that are not captured by simple measurements of kidney size and could help identify early signs of kidney disease before more obvious damage occurs

title: Cribriform Status at Follow-up Biopsy Is Critical for Predicting Prostate Cancer Active Surveillance Failure in the MRI Era: a Transatlantic Cohort Study
abstract: Purpose To assess whether follow-up MRI, biopsy status, and timing of cribriform disease detection predict active surveillance (AS) failure in a contemporary transatlantic cohort. Materials and Methods. Retrospective MRI-driven AS cohort of 619 men at two academic centers (UK/USA), 2012-2024. Primary outcome: AS failure (disease-specific mortality, metastasis, grade group [GG] ≥4 progression, or post-treatment biochemical recurrence). Key exposures: final MRI and biopsy status, timing of cribriform ≥GG2 detection. Cumulative incidence was derived; independent predictors used multivariable Fine-Gray models. Results. Over median follow-up of 6.4 years, 39/619 men (6%) experienced AS failure. Cribriform ≥GG2 was detected in 82/619 (13%) on follow-up biopsy versus 24/619 (4%) at baseline, comparably in baseline GG1 (10%) and non-cribriform GG2 (9%), and only in MRI-visible tumors. title: Optogenetic and sonogenetic pacing of unmodified cardiac tissue upon quick integration with specialized biological actuators
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrical stimulation for cardiac pacing has been in clinical use for 100 years and it is the current standard. Alternative scalable pacing methods that are contactless, with good spatial precision and can also be cell-selective are of interest for both in vitro and in vivo applications. Cardiac pacing by light or by ultrasound (US) can be achieved using optogenetic transduction of the tissue and by enhancing responsiveness to ultrasound. In this work we create specialized biological actuators (cell spheroids) out of generic human cells, modified optogenetically (using Channelrhodopsin2) and sonogenetically (using human Piezo1), guide them to a desired location to promote quick integration with unmodified cardiac syncytia within less than two hours. We quantify their ability to confer pacing by light or US and to entrain the native cardiac tissue, modeled here with human induced pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) grown in monolayers, quasi-3D oriented microtissues or cell spheroids. Magnetic guidance (via magnetic nanoparticles) speeds up integration and facilitates positioning to optimize electrotonic load for pacing; size match and three-dimensional growth also accelerate integration. Computational modeling corroborates the possibility to pace by light and by US. Using optogenetically-gated US pulses (0.5 MHz), we show entrainment in voltage and calcium responses and identify the best performing configurations. Experiments reveal the potential role of Piezo1, esp. when activated with Yoda1. The approach is shown to work with physiologically relevant heart cells, such as human cardiac fibroblasts as optimized actuators, and therefore can be considered for in vivo applications as part of heart regeneration efforts. High-throughput cardiotoxicity testing and drug screening in vitro can directly benefit from deployment of such biological actuators.

title: Ordinal Multi-Instance Learning for Automated Multi-Task Grading of Lumbar Degenerative Conditions on Sagittal MRI, with External Validation
abstract: Purpose: Lumbar spine MRI interpretation requires 25 structured severity judgments per examination (five degenerative conditions at five disc levels, each on a three-level ordinal scale), a time-consuming task with substantial inter-reader variability. We developed and externally validated a model that automates this complete scheme. Materials and Methods: A full-sequence multi-instance learning (MIL) model (ResNet34 backbone, bidirectional GRU, attention pooling over 24 uniformly sampled sagittal T2-weighted slices) with 25 cumulative-logit ordinal heads was trained on 1,204 examinations from the multi-institutional RSNA 2024 LumbarDISC dataset and internally validated on 213 held-out examinations. External validation used 60 retrospectively collected patients from an independent Chinese university hospital (four scanner vendors, radiology reports as the reference standard, no fine-tuning). Agreement was assessed with exact accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, McNemar tests, and patient-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. Results: The ordinal model achieved 51.4% balanced accuracy internally (exact accuracy 65.1%), versus 16.3% for a single-slice baseline; severe-grade AUCs averaged 0.908 across conditions. Externally, it outperformed its softmax-weighted counterpart on exact accuracy (0.649 vs. 0.586; +6.3 percentage points, 95% CI +2.7 to +10.0) and sensitivity (0.868 vs. 0.833), with markedly fewer severe-grade false alarms (69 vs. 172 predicted severe cells; McNemar p<0.0001). Conclusion: A full-sequence MIL model with ordinal outputs automates the complete 25-task grading scheme on sagittal MRI and, in the first hospital external validation of such a model, reduced severe-grade over-prediction under domain shift without loss of sensitivity, supporting its role as a screening and triage aid.

title: Proximal sesamoid bone fatigue in Thoroughbred racehorses is associated with palmar osteochondral disease in the adjacent third metacarpal bone condyle
abstract: Abstract Background: Proximal sesamoid bone (PSB) stress fracture is a common catastrophic injury in racing Thoroughbreds that is associated with bone sclerosis and development of focal osteolysis. Standing computed tomography (sCT) enables sensitive identification of these structural changes and associations with other more common fetlock fatigue injury such as palmar/plantar osteochondral disease lesions affecting the condyles of the third metacarpal/metatarsal (MC3/MT3). Objective: To gain insight into the PSB stress fracture mechanism, we examined associations between fatigue injury prevalence in the three major metacarpophalangeal (MCP) sites: PSB, parasagittal grooves (PSG), and third metacarpal bone MC3 condyles. Study design: Retrospective clinical study. Methods: We studied 22 catastrophically injured Thoroughbred racehorses. Thoracic limbs were examined using computed tomography (CT) (n=29). Subjective CT assessment classified 58 PSBs as 32 control and 26 case PSBs with bone fatigue (transverse fracture, focal osteolysis, or severe sclerosis). Opposing joint surfaces were also studied. PSB bone mineral density (BMD) was estimated. Results: Prevalence of fatigue injury in the PSB, condyle, and PSG was 44.8% (n=26), 43.1% (n=25), and 17.2% (n=10), respectively. For MC3 condyles with POD, 88.0% had fatigue injury in the corresponding PSB (OR = 53.2). Prevalence of PSB fatigue injury was 20.0% when there was PSG fatigue injury. The odds of a PSB having fatigue injury when the opposing MC3 PSG had signs of fatigue injury was 0.25. PSBs with opposing MC3 condyles containing a POD lesion had significantly increased BMD compared with opposing control condyles. BMD was significantly increased in PSBs with structural change associated with cyclic fatigue. Conclusions: Development of PSB fatigue and adaptive PSB sclerosis is associated with POD. Stress fractures in Thoroughbreds commonly affect the MCP joint. Condylar fractures occur from PSG or POD fatigue injury. PSB fractures are also common. Our findings suggest detailed clinical assessment of PSB structural change in racing Thoroughbreds diagnosed with POD is merited as part of routine injury prevention screening.

title: Structural damage of the cervical spinal cord within and beyond the maximal compression area in mucopolysaccharidosis types I and VI
abstract: BackgroundCervical spinal cord (CSC) compression and myelopathy are frequent, severe complications in mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and VI. Early detection is critical to prevent irreversible neurological deficits and preserve quality of life. This prospective study aimed to identify quantitative neuroimaging biomarkers of structural CSC damage and myelopathy in MPS I and VI. MethodsStructural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the CSC was analyzed in 17 MPS I patients, 3 MPS VI patients (19{+/-}7 years), and 19 case-matched healthy controls (20{+/-}7 years). CSC macrostructure (cross-sectional area, diameters) and microstructure (fractional anisotropy [FA], radial [RD], mean, axial diffusivities) were evaluated within and beyond the maximal compression areas. ResultsMPS patients demonstrated reduced CSC cross-sectional area and anterior-posterior diameter at upper cervical levels, alongside widespread microstructural alterations (lower FA, higher RD) throughout the CSC versus controls (pFDR<0.05). Restricted foramen magnum space was associated with microstructural damage at lower cervical levels without overt macrostructural compression. Morphological and microstructural metrics were sensitive to CSC compression and myelopathy severity (pFDR<0.05). Lower CSC integrity correlated with more advanced growth retardation (p<0.001). Among patients receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, earlier treatment correlated with preserved upper CSC morphology (p<0.05). Distinct neuroimaging phenotypes were observed across MPS genotypes (pFDR<0.05). ConclusionsCSC MRI provides candidate neuroimaging biomarkers for early detection and characterization of myelopathy in MPS I and VI. Structural damage extends beyond primary maximal compression areas, highlighting these markers for clinical monitoring and future therapeutic trials.

title: AI-Enhanced Segmentation and Scoring of Histopathological Growth Patterns in Resected Colorectal Liver Metastases
abstract: Histopathological growth patterns, predominantly the presence of an encapsulated rim, serve as powerful prognostic biomarkers in colorectal liver metastases. However, conventional visual estimation is limited by interobserver variability, human rounding bias, and categorical thresholds. We aimed to develop and externally validate a deep-learning segmentation framework that produces continuous, spatially resolved, and objective encapsulation metrics from routine whole-slide images. In this multicenter study of chemo-naive resected CRLM patients, a modified nnU-Net architecture was developed on 40 pixel-annotated H&E-stained WSIs to segment liver parenchyma, tumor, and the encapsulation interface. Model performance was optimized across spatial resolutions. An automated continuous AI encapsulation score was computed to determine patient-level metrics. The prognostic value for 5-year overall survival was evaluated using restricted cubic spline Cox regression, a log-rank optimized threshold, and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses across a main cohort (Erasmus MC; n=546, 1,910 WSIs) and an independent external validation cohort (Radboud UMC; n=212, 615 WSIs). The segmentation network achieved optimal tissue boundary delineation at a resolution of 2.0 micrometer/pixel on the 40 annotated slides (overall foreground DICE: 0.86+-0.09; encapsulation DICE: 0.70+-0.11). Spline modeling demonstrated that while visual assessment displayed non-linear hazard plateaus, the continuous AI encapsulation score exhibited a linear reduction in mortality risk across the critical intermediate range (25%-75% encapsulation, p=7.81x10^(-4)). Log-rank optimization identified a primary global threshold at 47.4% (p=3.73x10^(-8)), which in confirmed significant OS stratification in external validation (p=0.018). A secondary threshold was found at 69% (p=2.93x10^(-6)) that captured high-encapsulation favorable-risk patients matching the current manual 100% Rotterdam cut-off. Our deep-learning model transforms qualitative HGP grading into a continuous, explainable, and fully automated prognostic biometry. By eliminating observer subjectivity and capturing fine-grained risk gradients, the model establishes a scalable, standardized foundation for CRLM risk stratification on digital pathology.

title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
abstract: Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

title: Fine-tuned Medical Vision-Language Model (MedGemma 1.5 4B) with and without Structured Radiologist Descriptors versus EU-TIRADS for Malignancy Risk Stratification of Thyroid Nodules at Ultrasound: A Tunisian Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
abstract: Purpose. To evaluate a medical vision-language foundation model fine-tuned on thyroid ultrasound images, with or without the radiologist's structured descriptors, against expert-rated EU-TIRADS for the classification of thyroid nodules as benign or malignant. Materials and Methods. This retrospective study included nodules that underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) between January 2019 and August 2025 in two Tunisian centers, with consecutive recruitment, together with a selection of images from an international public dataset. Of 1,580 nodules, 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) with an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard were allocated at patient level to training (n = 942), validation (n = 258) and a test set sealed before training (n = 256; 51 malignant). MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations: the image with nodule biometry, with or without age and sex (A, B); A with chain-of-thought supervision (C); and A plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologist's structured report (D). The EU-TIRADS category was never a model input. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLong's test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS >= 4 was the prespecified comparator, with >= 5 as a sensitivity analysis. Results. Config D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At >= 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Against EU-TIRADS >= 5 (sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 95.1%), Config D at its native threshold (88.2%, 94.1%) did not classify more nodules correctly (McNemar p = 0.22), and at its two other thresholds it classified fewer nodules correctly (p = 0.004 and 0.007). Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040. Conclusion. Given the ultrasound image together with the radiologist's structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the >= 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation.

title: Loss of Farnesoid X Receptor Signaling Promotes Choroidal Neovascularization in Mice
abstract: Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is a defining feature of neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapies suppress neovascular activity, incomplete responses, recurrent leakage, and subretinal fibrosis remain important clinical challenges. The farnesoid X receptor (FXR) is a bile acid-activated nuclear receptor with anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and anti-angiogenic functions in other tissues, but its role in CNV is unknown. Analysis of publicly available human transcriptomic data (GSE135092) showed FXR expression in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/choroid and significant downregulation in AMD-affected macular RPE/choroid. To define the role of FXR in CNV, laser photocoagulation was performed in wild-type (WT) and FXR-deficient (FXR-KO) mice, with disease progression assessed by in vivo imaging, histology, ex vivo choroidal sprouting, and endothelial cell assays. FXR expression in the RPE/choroid was reduced 14 days after laser injury. Compared with WT mice, FXR-KO mice developed larger CNV lesions, more extensive hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography, and increased lesion area during disease progression. FXR deficiency also impaired resolution of fibrotic remodeling. In WT mice, alpha-SMA peaked at day 14 and declined by day 21, whereas collagen I remained low throughout; in FXR-KO mice, both collagen I and alpha-SMA were significantly elevated relative to WT and remained significantly higher than WT at day 21. Consistent with these findings, FXR-deficient choroidal explants exhibited increased vascular sprouting, and FXR-KO endothelial cells formed more extensive capillary-like networks. Together, these findings identify FXR as an endogenous regulator of pathological angiogenesis, vascular leakage, mesenchymal activation, and fibrotic remodeling during CNV and provide a rationale for investigating FXR-directed strategies for nAMD.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI for In-Hospital Detection of Lung Cancer and Heart Failure Using Routine Data: Development, Internal Validation, and Simulated Federated Evaluation
abstract: Objective: To determine whether combining four routine data sources improves in-hospital detection of lung cancer and heart failure, which sources drive each prediction, whether explanations are faithful, whether models are fair, and how much benefit federated training retains. Methods: In this retrospective single-centre study, we linked MIMIC-IV admissions (73,637 patients) to chest radiographs, radiology reports, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) and laboratory tests from the first 48 hours. For each disease, excluding prior cases, we compared single-source models, gradient boosting and early, late and attention-based fusion on patient-level splits. We tested explanations for faithfulness and weight dependence, audited performance by sex, age, race and ethnicity, and insurance, and simulated five unequal hospitals to compare federated, centralised and local training. Results: Lung cancer was coded in 1.7% and heart failure in 15.6% of patients. For lung cancer, attention fusion reached an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.833 (95% CI 0.809-0.859) against 0.753 for gradient boosting on laboratory data; for heart failure, 0.885 (0.878-0.892) against 0.794 (both p < 0.001). Early and late fusion performed similarly. Laboratory data and radiology reports contributed most to lung cancer, and the ECG to heart failure. Explanations passed a deletion test; a weight-randomisation check on absolute attributions passed for ECG but not for laboratory explanations. For heart failure, discrimination fell with age. Federated training recovered 95% of the centralised gain over local training for heart failure; for lung cancer, federated averaging (FedAvg) recovered 51% and FedProx 82%. Conclusion: Fusing routine data improved in-hospital detection of both diseases over laboratory data alone, and which data matter depends on the disease. Explanation checks should be run per source and per similarity measure, and performance in older patients monitored. For the rare outcome, FedProx, which limits drift between sites, retained more of the pooled benefit than FedAvg. External validation is needed.

title: Predicting HPV/p16 Status and Molecular Subtypes from Histopathology Slides using Deep Learning in Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) comprises three prognostically distinct molecular subtypes: human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated, HPV-independent/p53-wildtype, and HPV-independent/p53-abnormal. Classification requires p16/p53 immunohistochemistry, which consumes tissue and is often incomplete in retrospective cohorts. We investigated whether deep learning could predict HPV/p16 status and molecular subtypes directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. Using features extracted with H-optimus-1, we developed two attention-based multiple-instance learning models: HERA, predicting HPV/p16 status, and HERMES, predicting the three molecular subtypes. Models were developed on 644 patients from three Dutch VSCC cohorts and tested on 286 patients from two independent cohorts. In independent testing, HERA achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.75-0.91), with specificity 0.93, negative predictive value 0.94, and sensitivity 0.68. HERA-predicted groups reproduced the prognostic separation of HPV testing (log-rank p<0.001). HERMES achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.70 (0.66-0.75), with good discrimination for HPV-associated (0.80) but limited separation of HPV-independent/p53-abnormal (AUC 0.68) and HPV-independent/p53-wildtype (AUC 0.63). HERMES-predicted classes reproduced the prognostic hierarchy, with 5-year recurrence rates of 14.0% (HPV-associated), 31.1% (HPV-independent/p53-wildtype) and 43.3% (HPV-independent/p53-abnormal) (p=0.0051). Highly attended tiles showed basaloid cells and koilocytotic-like atypia in HPV-associated tumors, keratinizing nests with desmoplastic stroma in HPV-independent/p53-abnormal tumors, and well-differentiated keratinocytes with spongiosis in HPV-independent/p53-wildtype tumors. HERA could assign HPV/p16 status to large retrospective VSCC cohorts lacking ancillary testing, without consuming tissue, enabling HPV-stratified outcome analyses. Before such use, external validation of its discrimination and calibration across scanners and populations is required. HERMES suggests that molecular subtype information is encoded in hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, but requires improved distinction between the HPV-independent subtypes.

title: Feasibility study on using the diffusion-weighted imaging liver pulsation artifact as marker of liver fibrosis
abstract: Background: Liver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact. Purpose: This study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis. Study type: This study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers. Study population: Thirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included. Field Strength/Sequence: Imaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm2 and b800 = 800 s/mm2. Assessment: After manual segmentation of the left and right liver lobes, 18 first-order features were extracted from b50 and b800 images. We assumed the pulsation artifact was predominantly present in the left liver lobe in the b800 images. Thus, we computed the ratios of the intensity-normalized b800 features obtained from the left and right liver lobes. Additionally, we performed an intensity normalization to address the sometimes different signal intensities of left and right liver lobe. Then, we conducted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to differentiate cirrhotic from non- cirrhotic livers. Statistical tests: ROC analysis and leave-one-out bootstrapping were applied, both yielding area under the curve (AUC) values. Results: Left liver pulsation artifacts were more pronounced in non-cirrhotic livers and largely absent in cirrhotic livers. The first quartile feature, i.e. the first quartile of the normalized signal, best distinguished cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers (AUC = 0.95; 95% confidence interval 0.87-1.00). Data conclusion: The left liver DWI pulsation artifact reflects liver stiffness and could serve as a simple, intrinsic marker of liver cirrhosis. Analysis of the signal magnitude can differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

title: Quantized TotalSegmentator for Fast Abdominal Organ Segmentation on CPUs
abstract: BACKGROUND. TotalSegmentator is designed for a graphics processing unit (GPU), runs slowly on a central processing unit (CPU), and depends on Python, limiting CPU-only clinical deployment. OBJECTIVE. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether TS-Portable, a self-contained CPU executable running 8-bit integer (INT8)-quantized TotalSegmentator models, is noninferior to the reference implementation across 15 abdominal organs in an external multicenter cohort, quantify CPU-only runtime, and demonstrate spleen volumetry on a picture archiving and communication system (PACS) reading station. METHODS. This retrospective study compared TS-Portable with the reference Python implementation on 100 external multicenter CT scans and 28 chronic liver disease series. Per-case mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 3-mm normalized surface distance (NSD@3 mm) across 15 organs (1.5-mm resolution) and spleen-only mode were tested against a 0.01 noninferiority margin (paired bootstrap 95% CIs). Workstation and PACS runtimes were recorded; spleen volumes were compared via Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) and Bland-Altman analysis. RESULTS. The external cohort included 100 patients (53 men, 47 women; mean age, 53 {+/-} 16 [SD] years). Across 15 organs, TS-Portable was noninferior for mean DSC (difference, 0.00017; 95% CI, 0.00003 to 0.00031; p < .001) and NSD@3 mm (difference, 0.00015; 95% CI, -0.00002 to 0.00031; p < .001) and in spleen-only mode (both p < .001). Workstation 1.5-mm median runtime was 48.0 seconds for TS-Portable on CPU versus 342.5 seconds on CPU (ratio, 7.14) and 61.5 seconds on GPU (ratio, 1.28) for the reference. On PACS, CPU spleen volumetry took 5.8 versus 43.4 seconds, agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.9999; bias, 0.2%; 95% limits of agreement, -7.2% to 7.6%) and manual contours (CCC, 0.989; bias, -6.8%). In 28 chronic liver disease series, TS-Portable ran from DICOM in 6.5 seconds (median), agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.99999) and manual contours (CCC, 0.992; bias, -3.4%). CONCLUSION. TS-Portable achieved noninferior abdominal organ segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation while running faster on a workstation CPU than the reference on a GPU. CLINICAL IMPACT. Self-contained deployment enables fast multiorgan segmentation on CPU-only computers and spleen volumetry within seconds on a standard reading station, without dedicated GPUs or software installation.

title: Toward Electrical Impedance Tomography of Functional Activity in the Retina
abstract: Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) is a non-invasive electrical imaging technique that reconstructs spatial variations in tissue conductivity. Traditionally used for thoracic imaging, EIT has recently been extended to neural applications in the brain and peripheral nerves. This study investigates the feasibility of using EIT to image functional neural activity in the retina. We present computational modeling of EIT measurements for image reconstruction of small conductivity perturbations across different layers of the ex-vivo mouse retina with electrodes placed in epiretinal configuration. Experimentally, we describe the design of a multi-electrode array suitable for impedance measurements under these conditions and report preliminary recordings of light-evoked impedance changes in response to wide-field optical retinal stimulation. Our computational results suggest that small conductivity perturbations of 200µm diameter and 5% conductivity variation are experimentally detectable by high-end biopotential recording equipment and could be localized by EIT imaging within ≈13% of inter-electrode distance and ≈22% of retinal thickness, respectively. In preliminary recordings, we observed slow impedance variations of 13.0±9.3 µV (0.37±0.44%) in response to retina-wide light pulse trains, when performing impedance measurements with 10 µA applied current at 2-8 kHz. These variations were characterized by a slow time course, distinct from the fast neural EIT signals associated with action potentials, and may reflect extracellular or metabolic processes linked to retinal activation. Our modelling and technical results support the feasibility of retinal EIT, while the experimental observations are preliminary and motivate further controlled studies. Retinal EIT could significantly advance retinal electrophysiology research and prosthetic development.

title: An Extensive Tail Sign in Primary Thoracic Myxofibrosarcoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Myxofibrosarcoma is a malignant soft tissue tumor of fibroblastic origin, occurring mainly in the extremities but extremely rarely in the thoracic trunk. Myxofibrosarcoma typically appears as a slow-growing, painless mass but features a frequent local recurrence due to microscopic extension beyond visible margins. On MRI, the "tail sign"-which indicates subtle spread along the fascial plane-is known to be a potential risk factor for recurrence. Case presentation The patient was a 73-year-old woman complaining of continuous right back pain. Chest CT showed a poorly contrast-enhanced mass involving the 5th and 6th right ribs, as well as a separate nodule. The biopsy confirmed a diagnosis of myxofibrosarcoma. The mass exhibited hypointensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images on MRI; on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images and STIR images, a tail sign extending toward a small satellite nodule was observed. The patient underwent an extended resection involving the 5th through 7th ribs. A total of 61.2 Gy radiation was irradiated to the paravertebral region neighboring the tumor where the surgical margin was poor. A local recurrence was detected in the anterolateral region of the tumor resection site 5 months after surgery. The patient was treated with sequential chemotherapy using doxorubicin, eribulin, and pazopanib and is alive at 26 months after surgery without distant metastasis. Conclusions The current case exemplifies the aggressive local behavior of thoracic myxofibrosarcoma, especially when a long tail sign appears.

title: Hepatic Metastasis of Meningioma Treated with Partial Hepatectomy: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Meningioma is one of the most common central nervous system tumors; however, metastatic lesions are extremely rare. Particularly, hepatic metastasis from meningioma is uncommon, and its diagnosis and optimal management remain undefined. Case presentation A 70-year-old man with a history of left parietal meningioma resection in 2011 and gamma knife therapy for recurrence in the left lateral ventricle in June 2025. A PET-CT scan performed for cancer screening in June 2025 revealed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in segment 8 of the liver, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 6.2. CT, and MRI revealed multiple hepatic masses. All tumor markers were within normal ranges. A percutaneous liver biopsy indicated a spindle cell tumor; however, the diagnosis remained inconclusive. For diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, partial hepatectomy of segments 6 and 8 and cholecystectomy were performed. Histopathological examination revealed proliferating spindle-shaped tumor cells arranged in fascicles. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for vimentin, epithelial membrane antigen, and somatostatin receptor 2, confirming the diagnosis of hepatic metastasis from meningioma. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged in good condition. Conclusions Hepatic metastasis from meningioma is extremely rare; however, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of hepatic tumors in patients with a history of meningioma. Surgical resection is valuable in establishing a definitive diagnosis and achieving local disease control.

title: A Case of Primary Leiomyoma of the Chest Wall Showing High Uptake on FDG-PET.
abstract: Introduction Primary leiomyoma of the chest wall is a rare entity. We report a case of primary chest wall leiomyoma with intense uptake on fluorodeoxyglucose PET (FDG-PET), requiring differentiation from malignancy. Case presentation An 82-year-old man with a history of asbestos exposure underwent annual chest CT surveillance. A 19-mm nodule was newly identified on the right chest wall and had not been present on CT the previous year. Although the lesion had well-defined margins on CT, FDG-PET demonstrated intense uptake with a maximum standardized uptake value of 11.8, raising suspicion for malignancy. Surgical resection was performed for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Histopathological examination revealed fascicular proliferation of spindle-shaped cells. Immunohistochemical analysis suggested a smooth muscle tumor, and retention of BRCA1-associated protein 1 and methylthioadenosine phosphorylase excluded mesothelioma. Based on these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a primary leiomyoma of the chest wall. Conclusions Primary leiomyomas of the chest wall are rare and may show high FDG uptake on PET imaging, making differentiation from malignant tumors challenging. A comprehensive evaluation incorporating imaging, intraoperative findings, and pathological assessment is essential for accurate diagnosis.

title: Small Bowel Volvulus Diagnosed and Treated Using Intraoperative Angiography in a Hybrid Operating Room: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Small bowel volvulus is a surgical emergency that may cause mesenteric ischemia; however, diagnosis may be difficult when bowel perfusion appears preserved. Case presentation An 84-year-old man presented with recurrent postprandial abdominal pain and melena 6 months after a total pharyngolaryngectomy with a jejunal free flap reconstruction. Extensive endoscopic evaluations, including capsule endoscopy, revealed no bleeding source. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed the whirl sign at the root of the small-bowel mesentery with the narrowing of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), while bowel wall enhancement was preserved. Because the symptoms recurred after resuming oral intake, a hybrid surgery combined with angiography was planned for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The SMA angiography demonstrated significant stenosis without apparent bowel hypoperfusion. After the intra-arterial administration of alprostadil, distal mesenteric perfusion deteriorated on the angiography, and laparoscopic exploration revealed ischemic changes consistent with small bowel volvulus. Because laparoscopic reduction was difficult, an open reduction was performed. Repeat angiography confirmed the resolution of the SMA narrowing and the restoration of distal flow. The patient's symptoms resolved completely. Conclusions The hybrid surgery enabled a functional assessment of mesenteric hemodynamics and immediate surgical treatment during a single procedure. It may be useful in selected patients with small bowel volvulus who have preserved bowel perfusion at rest but recurrent symptoms suggestive of intermittent mesenteric ischemia, and in whom the indication for surgical detorsion remains uncertain.
