title: A Case of a Cardiac Re-Rupture Caused by the Removal of Pericardial Patches Late after a Sutureless Repair for a Cardiac Rupture.
abstract: Introduction Surgical treatment is the only reliable therapeutic option for a left ventricular free wall rupture (LVFWR). There are 2 major surgical techniques, namely, sutureless repair and sutured repair; a ventricular pseudoaneurysm is a late postoperative complication. We herein report a case of a re-ruptured left ventricular pseudoaneurysm after a sutureless bovine pericardial patch repair. Case presentation The patient was a 79-year-old woman who underwent a sutureless pericardial patch repair for a blow-out-type left ventricular rupture following an anterior myocardial infarction 10 months previously. She was referred to Fujita Health University Okazaki Medical Center with a diagnosis of thoracic empyema and a suspected pericardial patch infection. Pleural effusion was positive for a few Streptococcus agalactiae . Coronary CT revealed the occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending branch and aneurysmal dilatation of the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle covered with pericardial patches. The operation was performed via a left fifth intercostal thoracotomy without cardiopulmonary bypass. The covering bovine pericardial patches and felt strips were easily removed, and the omental flap was secured in place. However, an emergency reoperation was necessitated for a left hemothorax 3 hours after surgery. Active bleeding was observed from the aneurysmal area, which had been previously covered with pericardial patches. After inducing deep hypothermia of 20°C, the fragile tissue surrounding the bleeding site was debrided under ventricular fibrillation. A 3 × 3-cm myocardial tissue defect was observed and closed using a bovine pericardial patch (Model 4700; Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, CA, USA) with ten 2-0 MH U sutures (ETHIBOND EXCEL polyester suture, 2-0, MH needle, X843H; Ethicon, Somerville, NJ, USA). All intraoperative cultures were negative, and the fragile tissue revealed an organizing hematoma lacking any myocardial tissue. She experienced prolonged respiratory failure, requiring tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation for 6 months, and was moved to the rehabilitation ward, but died 1 year after surgery due to pneumonia. Conclusions Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm formation is a notable late complication that should be carefully monitored during the postoperative follow-up after surgery for LVFWR. We encountered a case of a re-ruptured left ventricular pseudoaneurysm after a sutureless bovine pericardial patch repair. The possibility of re-rupture must be considered because the myocardial tissue beneath the pericardial patch might disappear and be replaced with an organizing hematoma.

title: Confluence Stones at the Junction of the Cystic Duct and an Aberrant Anterior Sectoral Bile Duct: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Confluence stones usually arise when gallstones impacted in the cystic duct migrate toward the biliary confluence. Surgical treatment can be technically demanding because of chronic inflammation and distorted anatomy. Confluence stones at the junction between the cystic duct and an aberrant bile duct are extremely rare. We report a successfully treated case of confluence stones arising at the junction of the cystic duct and an aberrant anterior sectoral bile duct with a communicating accessory bile duct. Case presentation A 38-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain, and biliary stones were detected. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated an aberrant anterior sectoral bile duct draining independently into the common bile duct. Biliary stones were identified both within this duct and at its junction with the cystic duct. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography confirmed the biliary anatomy and additionally revealed a communicating accessory bile duct between the anterior and posterior sectoral ducts. The stones within the distal portion of the aberrant duct were removed endoscopically, but the impacted confluence stones could not be extracted. Therefore, open surgery was performed. After exposure of the junction, the confluence stones were removed through a semicircumferential incision. Complete stone clearance was confirmed by intraoperative cholangioscopy and cholangiography. The patient was discharged on POD 11 with no bile leakage. At 14 months postoperatively, she remained asymptomatic and had experienced no episodes of cholangitis. Conclusions We report a rare case of confluence stones arising at the junction of the cystic duct and an aberrant anterior sectoral bile duct. Preoperative assessment of the drainage territory and intraoperative evaluation of the duct diameter, ischemia, and tissue fragility are essential for appropriate and safe repair of the bile duct defect. The repair strategy should not rely on presumed bypass flow through a communicating accessory bile duct because its functional capacity cannot be reliably predicted.

title: Pancreaticoduodenectomy after Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy with Preservation of Gastric Arterial Inflow: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Obesity is an established risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. As laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) has become increasingly prevalent, pancreatic surgeons may encounter malignancies in patients with a surgically altered gastric anatomy. Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) after an LSG is rare and requires meticulous preoperative planning to prevent ischemic and anastomotic complications. Case presentation A 47-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI 59.1 kg/m 2 ) underwent LSG. Twenty-three days later, obstructive jaundice led to the diagnosis of pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy and substantial weight reduction (BMI 34.9 kg/m 2 ), subtotal stomach-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy with wedge resection of the superior mesenteric vein was performed. Preoperative CT confirmed the preservation and patency of both the left and right gastric arteries. The left gastric artery was preserved intraoperatively. Gastrojejunostomy was performed using a hand-sewn anastomosis between the greater curvature side of the sleeve stomach and the jejunum. The patient developed a grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula but was discharged with no ischemic complications. Conclusions PD after an LSG is feasible, but careful vascular assessment, a preplanned reconstruction strategy, consideration of the patient's metabolic and nutritional status, and careful intraoperative assessment of the remnant stomach may enhance surgical safety.

title: Resection of a Large Intra-Abdominal Desmoid Tumor with Preoperative Superior Mesenteric Artery Balloon Catheter Placement: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Large tumors occupying the abdominal cavity can hinder surgical exposure, particularly of the posterior aspect, increasing the risk of arterial bleeding. Because arterial hemostasis is difficult, hemodynamic instability may occur. This report describes the safe use of preoperative balloon catheter placement in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), the tumor's primary feeding vessel, to control arterial bleeding through on-demand intraoperative occlusion. Case presentation A 40-year-old woman with a history of 2 cesarean sections presented with abdominal distension. An intra-abdominal mass was identified at another institution, and she was referred to our hospital. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a large intra-abdominal mass supplied primarily by jejunal branches of the SMA. US-guided biopsy confirmed desmoid tumor. Chemotherapy was also considered; however, debulking surgery followed by chemotherapy was planned to relieve abdominal symptoms. Because the large tumor was expected to limit surgical exposure and increase the risk of intraoperative bleeding, an SMA balloon catheter was electively placed the day before surgery. During surgery, the balloon was inflated on demand by the anesthesiologist at the surgeon's direction before maneuvers carrying a risk of arterial bleeding. Tumor involvement of the small bowel mesentery, transverse mesocolon, small intestine, and duodenum required en bloc resection. As SMA involvement was confined to the segment distal to the ileocolic artery bifurcation, complete macroscopic resection was feasible while preserving approximately 200 cm of the small bowel. The resected specimen weighed 5660 g. Immunohistochemistry showed nuclear β-catenin positivity, confirming the diagnosis of desmoid tumor. Negative surgical margins achieved R0 resection. One year later, MRI detected a 1.5-cm intra-abdominal recurrence in the right upper abdomen. Chemotherapy achieved stable disease after 7 months but was discontinued because of nausea and vomiting. At 3 years postoperatively, no disease progression has been observed. Conclusions In large intra-abdominal desmoid tumors with anticipated limited surgical exposure, preoperative SMA balloon catheter placement may facilitate arterial-bleeding control and improve surgical safety.

title: Gastric Glomus Tumor Mimicking a Neuroendocrine Tumor: A Case Report Highlighting Diagnostic Pitfalls.
abstract: Introduction Gastric glomus tumors (GGTs) are rare mesenchymal neoplasms arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body. Their subepithelial location and pronounced hypervascularity overlap considerably with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) and neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) on imaging and in small biopsy specimens, making an accurate preoperative diagnosis challenging; as a result, such lesions are frequently diagnosed after surgical resection. Case presentation A 38-year-old asymptomatic woman was found to have a 25-mm well-circumscribed, hypervascular submucosal lesion with a small central depression and minute ulceration in the upper gastric body during a routine health-screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) demonstrated a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass arising from the third sonographic layer without evidence of muscularis propria invasion. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a hypervascular lesion with no regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis. Conventional forceps biopsies targeting the minute ulceration, evaluated with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining alone, were interpreted as consistent with a NET, leading to a provisional diagnosis of a type III gastric NET. Because of the diagnostic uncertainty surrounding the NET diagnosis, and because the EUS and CT showed no evidence of deep or nodal spread, the patient underwent laparoscopic and endoscopic cooperative surgery (LECS) with a local full-thickness gastric resection rather than upfront gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy, and the defect was repaired through a protective mini-laparotomy. Definitive histopathology demonstrated uniform round-to-spindle cells arranged in a perivascular sheet pattern within a myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed focal positivity for α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and negativity for KIT (CD117), CD34, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, desmin, and the S-100 protein, confirming a GGT. All surgical margins were negative, and no recurrence has been observed over 5 years of follow-up. Conclusions A GGT must be included in the differential diagnosis of hypervascular gastric subepithelial lesions (SELs), including those with a nested, NET-like architecture. H&E staining alone is insufficient for a definitive diagnosis; direct communication with the pathologist and comprehensive IHC profiling are indispensable. LECS is a favorable and effective organ-preserving strategy for localized gastric SELs when the diagnosis remains uncertain despite the preoperative evaluation.

title: Pancreatic Perivascular Epithelioid Cell Tumor: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Introduction Perivascular epithelioid cell tumors (PEComas) are rare mesenchymal neoplasms, and primary pancreatic PEComas are exceptionally uncommon. Owing to their rarity, the prognostic significance of their pathological features remains unclear. We report a resected case of pancreatic PEComa and review the literature to further characterize its clinicopathological features. Case presentation A 72-year-old woman presented with a gradually enlarging, 63-mm hypervascular tumor in the pancreatic body. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed hypervascular mass with central hypoenhancement, suggestive of coagulative necrosis. Endoscopic US-guided tissue acquisition suggested acinar cell carcinoma because of weak trypsin positivity, and distal pancreatectomy with regional lymph node dissection was performed. Histopathological examination of the resected specimen revealed epithelioid and spindle cells that were positive for HMB45 and Melan-A and weakly positive for α-smooth muscle actin, leading to a diagnosis of pancreatic PEComa. The patient remained disease-free at 18 months after surgery. We also reviewed 26 previously reported cases of pancreatic PEComa and re-evaluated those with sufficient pathological information according to the Folpe criteria. Metastasis developed in 1 tumor classified as malignant and 1 classified as having uncertain malignant potential. Coagulative necrosis and increased mitotic activity appeared to be more frequent in the 2 metastatic cases; however, the small number of events precluded conclusions regarding their prognostic significance or the predictive performance of the Folpe classification. Conclusions Pancreatic PEComa should be considered in the differential diagnosis of hypervascular pancreatic tumors with atypical immunophenotypic findings. Additional immunohistochemical staining for melanocytic markers may facilitate an accurate preoperative diagnosis. The prognostic significance of individual pathological features and the applicability of the Folpe classification to pancreatic PEComa remain uncertain and require evaluation in additional well-documented cases with long-term follow-up.

title: Impact of FOSL1 polymorphisms and expression on disease progression in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) is the most common subtype of oral cancer, with betel quid chewing, tobacco smoking, and alcohol consumption recognized as major risk factors. This study investigated the associations between FOSL1 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and disease susceptibility and clinicopathological characteristics in OTSCC patients. Three FOSL1 SNPs (rs637571, rs653914, and rs10896065) were genotyped in 377 male OTSCC patients and 1,194 controls using real-time polymerase chain reaction. The FOSL1 rs10896065 polymorphic T variant was significantly associated with advanced clinical stage (Stage III-IV; AOR = 1.663, 95% CI = 1.059-2.611, p = 0.027) and larger tumor size (AOR = 1.813, 95% CI = 1.162-2.831, p = 0.009). Among betel quid chewers, carriers of the CT+TT genotype showed significant associations with advanced clinical stage, larger tumor size, and moderate-to-poor tumor differentiation. Similar associations with advanced stage and greater tumor size were observed among smokers carrying the CT+TT genotype. Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas dataset further demonstrated that elevated FOSL1 mRNA expression was significantly associated with larger tumor size (T3-T4 vs. T1-T2, p = 0.0216). These findings suggest that the FOSL1 rs10896065 T allele is associated with advanced clinicopathological features in OTSCC patients, particularly among betel-quid chewers and smokers. FOSL1 polymorphisms may have potential as biomarkers associated with clinicopathological characteristics in OTSCC.

title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.
abstract: Background The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). Objective To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. Design Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. Setting Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. Participants No human participants were involved. Measurements Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). Results The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). Limitations Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. Conclusion The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. Primary funding source None.

title: [Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with double-bundle artificial ligament based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism: a comparative study with single-bundle reconstruction].
abstract: Objective To investigate the surgical method of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction with double-bundle artificial ligaments based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism, and to compare its short-term effectiveness with traditional single-bundle reconstruction. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 45 patients with complete ACL rupture who met the selection criteria and were treated between October 2022 and October 2025. Based on anatomical measurement results and surgical technique selection, patients were divided into a single-bundle reconstruction group (29 cases, receiving traditional over-the-top isometric single-bundle reconstruction) and a double-bundle reconstruction group [16 cases, receiving four-dimensional impingement free ACL double-bundle reconstruction (over-the-top anteromedial bundle+low posterolateral bundle)]. Baseline data-including age, injured side, cause of injury, concomitant meniscus injury, and preoperative Lysholm score, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) score, and Tegner score-showed no significant difference between the two groups ( P >0.05); however, the difference in gender distribution between the two groups was significant ( P <0.05). Operation time, complications, knee range of motion, and the results of the Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot-shift test were recorded. Knee function was evaluated using the Lysholm, IKDC, and Tegner scores preoperatively and at last follow-up, and the proportion of patients returning to pre-injury sports activity levels was calculated. Postoperative three-dimensional CT was performed to evaluate bone tunnel placement and graft-to-tunnel congruence. Results Operations were successfully completed in both groups, with the operation time in the double-bundle reconstruction group being significantly longer than that in the single-bundle reconstruction group ( P <0.05). All patients were followed up 6-13 months, with an average of 8.5 months. Patients in both groups resumed immediate postoperative knee range of motion reached 0°-135°, and normal independent walking at 2 weeks postoperatively. At last follow-up, the Lachman test and anterior drawer test were negative in all patients; the pivot-shift test was negative in all cases in the double-bundle reconstruction group, whereas 3 cases (all grade Ⅰ) were positive in the single-bundle reconstruction group, with no significant difference in the positive rate of the pivot-shift test between the two groups ( P >0.05). At last follow-up, the proportion of patients returning to pre-injury sports activity levels was significantly higher in the double-bundle reconstruction group than in the single-bundle reconstruction group ( P <0.05). Both the IKDC and Tegner scores showed significant improvement compared with preoperative values in the two groups ( P <0.05), while the Lysholm scores showed no significant difference when compared with preoperative values ( P >0.05). There was no significant difference in the pre- to post-operative change values of each score between the two groups ( P >0.05). Postoperative three-dimensional CT demonstrated that the distance between the margins of the anterior and posterior bone tunnels in the double-bundle reconstruction group was more than 5 mm, with no evidence of tunnel fracture or posterior cruciate ligament impingement; MRI showed favorable graft morphology without signs of impingement. During the follow-up, no severe complications such as graft laxity, rupture, or synovitis occurred in either group. Conclusion Under the guarantee of strict anatomical screening, artificial ligament double-bundle reconstruction based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism shows a favorable clinical trend in restoring rotational stability, with pivot-shift control superior to that of single-bundle reconstruction. Combined with a higher rate of return to sports, it holds significant clinical value for athletic populations seeking early, high-quality rehabilitation. Knee function was evaluated using the Lysholm, IKDC, and Tegner scores preoperatively and at last follow-up, and the proportion of patients returning to pre-injury sports activity levels was calculated. Postoperative three-dimensional CT was performed to evaluate bone tunnel placement and graft-to-tunnel congruence.

Under the guarantee of strict anatomical screening, artificial ligament double-bundle reconstruction based on four-dimensional impingement free mechanism shows a favorable clinical trend in restoring rotational stability, with pivot-shift control superior to that of single-bundle reconstruction. Combined with a higher rate of return to sports, it holds significant clinical value for athletic populations seeking early, high-quality rehabilitation. However, strict indication screening based on individualized anatomical conditions is essential for this surgical procedure.

title: [Effectiveness comparison of one-hole split endoscopy and unilateral biportal endoscopy discectomy via the superior articular process approach for L 5 , S 1 far lateral lumbar disc herniation].
abstract: Objective To compare the effectiveness between one-hole split endoscopy(OSE) and unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE) discectomy via the superior articular process approach for L 5 , S 1 far lateral lumbar disc herniation (FLLDH). Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on the clinical data of 98 patients with L 5 , S 1 FLLDH who met the selection criteria and were admitted between January 2021 and December 2024. The patients were divided into an OSE group (52 cases) and a UBE group (46 cases) according to the surgical procedure. There was no significant difference in baseline data between the two groups ( P >0.05), such as age, gender, side, body mass index, preoperative anterior-posterior translation distance (ATD), disc height (DH), lumbar lordosis angle (LLA), visual analogue scale (VAS) scores for low back pain and leg pain, and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Operation time, intraoperative blood loss, intraoperative fluoroscopy frequency, incision length, and postoperative hospital stay were recorded. Three-dimensional lumbar models were reconstructed, and the proportion of resected superior articular process bone volume of S 1 was calculated by measuring the bone volume of the S 1 superior articular process before and after surgery. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using VAS scores, ODI, while lumbar stability was assessed by ATD, DH, and LLA measurements. Results All patients successfully underwent operation. The OSE group had significantly shorter operation time, less intraoperative blood loss, and smaller incision length than the UBE group ( P <0.05); no significant difference was found in intraoperative fluoroscopy frequency or postoperative hospital stay between the two groups ( P >0.05). No severe neurological or vascular injuries occurred intraoperatively in either group, mild dural tears were observed in 2 patients in the UBE group. All patients were followed up 12-18 months, with an average of 14.7 months. In both groups, VAS scores and ODI at each postoperative time point decreased significantly when compared with preoperative values, with further improvement over time, and the differences among time points were significant ( P <0.05). Intergroup comparisons showed that, except for a higher low back pain VAS score in the UBE group at postoperative 3 days ( P <0.05), there was no significant difference in VAS scores or ODI between the two groups at the other time points ( P >0.05). At last follow-up, there was no significant difference in ATD, DH, and LLA within each group when compared with preoperative values ( P >0.05). No significant intergroup difference was observed in the changes of ATD, DH, and LLA from preoperation to postoperation between the two groups ( P >0.05). There was a significant difference in the proportion of resected superior articular processbone volume of S 1 between the two groups ( P <0.05), but the proportion in both groups were less than 35%. There was no recurrence during the follow-up. Conclusion Both OSE and UBE approaches for lumbar discectomy via the superior articular process can achieve satisfactory effectiveness for treating L 5 , S 1 FLLDH, preserve more important bone of the S 1 superior articular process, which is conducive to maintaining lumbar stability. Compared with UBE, the OSE technique offers advantages of shorter operation time, less trauma, and reduced blood loss.

title: [Comparative study on effectiveness of two fixation methods in treatment of mid-column plantar-flexion Lisfranc injuries].
abstract: Objective To compare the effectiveness of open reduction with screw internal fixation versus primary arthrodesis for mid-column plantar-flexion Lisfranc injuries. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 45 patients (45 feet) with mid-column plantar-flexion Lisfranc injuries, who met the selective criteria between June 2019 and June 2022. Among them, 23 patients were treated with primary tarsometatarsal arthrodesis (arthrodesis group), and 22 patients received open reduction with screw internal fixation (screw group). There was no significant difference between groups ( P >0.05) in age, gender, body mass index, injured side, interval from injury to operation, Myerson classification, and preoperative visual analogue scale (VAS) score, American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, 36-Item Short-Form Health Survey (SF-36) score, the distance between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal (C1-M2), the distance between first and second metatarsal (M1-M2), step-off sign (SOS) displacement, and talus-first metatarsal angle (Meary angle). Operation time, incision length, intraoperative fluoroscopy frequency, intraoperative blood loss, time to initial weight-bearing, time to full weight-bearing, and postoperative complications during follow-up were recorded and compared. Pain and functional recovery were evaluated using VAS, AOFAS, and SF-36 scores. Radiographic parameters including C1-M2, M1-M2, SOS displacement, and Meary angle were measured during follow-up. Intergroup differences in the changes of the all outcome indicators from preoperative to last follow-up were also compared. Results All patients underwent successful operation. The arthrodesis group had significantly longer operation time, longer incision length, more intraoperative fluoroscopy exposures, and greater intraoperative blood loss compared with the screw group ( P <0.05). All patients were followed up 24-36 months (mean, 27.6 months). No significant intergroup difference was found in time to initial weight-bearing or time to full weight-bearing ( P >0.05). At last follow-up, the indicators for function, pain, and imaging in both groups significantly improved compared with those before operation ( P <0.05). The arthrodesis group achieved significantly greater changes of AOFAS score, VAS score, SF-36 score, and Meary angle than the screw group ( P <0.05). No significant intergroup difference was found in the changes of C1-M2, M1-M2, and SOS ( P >0.05). The incidence of complication was significantly lower in arthrodesis group (8.6%, 2/23) than in screw group (36.3%, 8/22) ( P <0.05). Conclusion For mid-column plantar-flexion Lisfranc injuries, primary tarsometatarsal arthrodesis yields better functional recovery and pain relief compared with open reduction and screw internal fixation.

title: [Effectiveness of arthroscopic grid-pattern dynamic rotator cuff reconstruction using autologous tendon graft for irreparable massive rotator cuff tears].
abstract: Objective To evaluate effectiveness of arthroscopic grid-pattern dynamic rotator cuff reconstruction using autologous tendon graft in treatment of irreparable massive rotator cuff tears (IMRCT). Methods A retrospective case series study was conducted on 32 patients with IMRCT treated between July 2022 and December 2023. All patients underwent arthroscopic grid-pattern dynamic rotator cuff reconstruction using autologous peroneus longus tendon graft. There were 11 males and 21 females, aged 49-76 years (mean, 65 years). The clinical symptoms were joint pain accompanied by limited mobility and abduction weakness. The duration of preoperative symptoms ranged from 3 to 24 months (mean, 9 months). Pain was assessed using the visual analogue scale (VAS) score, and shoulder function was evaluated using the modified University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA) score and the Constant-Murley score before operation and at 3, 6, 12 months after operation. MRI was performed during follow-up to assess graft integrity. Complications were recorded. Results The operation time ranged from 75 to 130 minutes, with a mean of 90 minutes. All incisions healed by first intention, and no significant complication or adverse reaction was observed. All patients were followed up 12-24 months (mean, 16.5 months). All postoperative scores improved significantly when compared with preoperative values ( P <0.05). Pain and function continued to improve over time; no significant difference was observed in the modified UCLA scores among 6 months, 12 months, and last follow-up, nor in any scores between 12 months and last follow-up ( P >0.05); all other pairwise comparisons showed significant differences ( P <0.05). At last follow-up, shoulder function was rated as excellent in 12 cases, good in 18 cases, and poor in 2 cases according to the modified UCLA scoring system, yielding an excellent-to-good rate of 93.8%. MRI follow-up demonstrated intact reconstructed rotator cuff structures in 29 patients, with a healing rate of 90.6% (29/32). Conclusion Arthroscopic grid-pattern dynamic rotator cuff reconstruction using autologous tendon graft is effective for IMRCT, significantly alleviating pain, improving shoulder range of motion, and restoring both functional and structural integrity, without major complication or adverse reaction.

title: Comparison of Data-Driven Phenotyping Systems for metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: Implications for Treatment Response.
abstract: Background Although emerging classification systems address the pathophysiological heterogeneity of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), the implications of these subtypes for treatment responses remain unclear. We systematically evaluated three phenotyping frameworks for stratifying responses to lifestyle management. Methods This prospective observational cohort study included 618 patients with MASLD who received 48 weeks of guideline-based lifestyle management. The classification systems assessed were metabolic clusters-mild obesity/dyslipidemia-associated MASLD (MODM), age-related MASLD (AM), severe insulin resistance-associated MASLD, high lipoprotein(a)-associated MASLD (HLPAM), and severe mixed hyperlipidemia-associated MASLD (SMHLM); hepatic and cardiometabolic traits (control, liver-specific, and cardiometabolic); and biochemical patterns (hepatocellular, mixed, and cholestatic). The primary endpoints were responses in magnetic resonance imaging-derived proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) (≥30% relative liver fat reduction), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (≥17 IU/L decrease), and liver stiffness measurements (LSM) (≥1-stage improvement in the LSM-defined fibrosis stage). Results Metabolic clusters demonstrated significantly greater temporal stability than the hepatic and cardiometabolic trait and biochemical pattern systems (62.8% vs. 56.6% vs. 53.4%, P =0.003). The HLPAM cluster demonstrated an attenuated MRI-PDFF response (odds ratio [OR], 0.35; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.15 to 0.79), while the AM cluster showed a lower ALT response (OR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.18 to 0.62), and the MODM cluster displayed a superior LSM response compared to the others (all P <0.05). Moreover, the liver-specific cluster showed better MRI-PDFF, ALT, and LSM responses than the control cluster. However, biochemical patterns selectively stratified ALT responses, with the hepatocellular pattern demonstrating a greater response than the mixed and cholestatic patterns. Conclusion Metabolic cluster-based MASLD subtypes exhibited differential responses to lifestyle management, supporting the integration of metabolic subtyping into clinical algorithms to optimize management.

title: Three-dimensional coded aperture imaging system proposed for early breast cancer detection using low tumor-to-background ratio.
abstract: Coded aperture (CA) based image formation methods have been used in medical imaging for the past two decades. However, no commercially available Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) CA camera technology has been developed yet. This study investigated the lower tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) in 3D breast reconstruction with tumors. TBR is a potential factor for evaluating the malignancy of breast cancer because of its correlation with lesion size. The CA-based SPECT camera uses an iterative reconstruction algorithm called Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) with a mosaic Modified Uniformly Redundant Array (MURA) mask and anti-mask dual reconstruction. The background noise and intrinsic artifacts are suppressed by subtracting mask reconstructed images from the anti-mask images, thereby reducing the non-uniformity in the background. The reconstructed slices are then stacked to create a three-dimensional representation of the breast phantom. By employing a TBR of 5:1, mosaic MURA mask anti-mask subtraction has enhanced the quality of the reconstructed images and made it possible to detect breast lesions with a diameter of 4 mm. Furthermore, rather than using a sinogram, the proposed method can create a 3D breast phantom from a single projection. Simulation results suggest the feasibility of detecting 4 mm lesions at TBR = 5:1 using a single-projection mosaic MURA coded aperture system. Clinical validation is required to confirm translation to patient imaging.

title: Colonic Angiosarcoma 16 Years After Pelvic Radiotherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Case Report.
abstract: Angiosarcomas are rare and aggressive malignant neoplasms of vascular or lymphatic endothelial origin, accounting for approximately 2% of soft-tissue sarcomas. They occur predominantly in the skin and superficial soft tissues, particularly in the head and neck region and the breast, whereas gastrointestinal involvement is exceptionally rare. Previous radiotherapy is a well-established risk factor for secondary angiosarcoma. However, radiation-associated gastrointestinal angiosarcomas are extremely uncommon and have been reported predominantly in the small bowel. We report the case of a 55-year-old woman who presented with abdominal pain, hemorrhagic ascites, intermittent rectal bleeding, severe anemia, anorexia, and weight loss 16 years after pelvic radiotherapy and cisplatin-based chemotherapy for cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Computed tomography revealed circumferential thickening of the cecum and right colon with abundant hyperdense ascites. Colonoscopy showed an obstructing, ulcerated, and contact-bleeding mass involving the cecum and right colon. Histopathological examination of endoscopic biopsies revealed a poorly differentiated malignant vascular neoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cluster of differentiation (CD)31 and CD34 and negative for cytokeratin, CD3, CD20, and Human Herpesvirus (HHV)8, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 40%, supporting the diagnosis of colonic angiosarcoma. Surgical resection was considered; however, the patient developed a massive bilateral pulmonary embolism and died seven days after admission. Given the prolonged latency and the histological distinction from the primary cervical carcinoma, a possible radiation-associated etiology was considered. Nevertheless, the original radiotherapy plan was unavailable, preventing definitive confirmation that the tumor arose within the irradiated field. This case highlights the diagnostic difficulty, aggressive clinical course, and poor prognosis of colonic angiosarcoma following pelvic radiotherapy.

title: When Hypercapnia Misleads: A Case of Respiratory-Onset Motor Neuron Disease.
abstract: Motor neuron disease (MND) most commonly presents with limb or bulbar weakness; however, a minority of patients present with respiratory-onset disease, posing significant diagnostic challenges. We report the case of a 78-year-old woman with a background of small airways disease and rheumatoid arthritis not requiring treatment for many years, who presented with a two-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, unintentional weight loss, and functional decline. Before diagnosis, she underwent extensive investigation across primary and secondary care, including chest radiography, spirometry, computed tomography imaging, and ear, nose, and throat specialist assessment, without a unifying diagnosis being established. On admission, venous blood gas demonstrated compensated hypercapnia, which was attributed to obstructive airways disease. She subsequently developed hypercapnic respiratory failure, and a clinical diagnosis of MND was made on the basis of generalised muscle wasting, fasciculations, brisk lower-limb reflexes, and electromyography findings. Non-invasive ventilation was initiated with significant clinical improvement. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of respiratory-onset MND, the risk of anchoring bias in the interpretation of biochemical markers, and the importance of considering neuromuscular causes when respiratory symptoms are disproportionate to radiological and biochemical findings.

We report the case of a 78-year-old woman with a background of small airways disease and rheumatoid arthritis not requiring treatment for many years, who presented with a two-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, unintentional weight loss, and functional decline. title: Solitary Rectal Ulcer Syndrome Mimicking Ulcerative Colitis: A Case Report.
abstract: Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome (SRUS) is a benign rectal disorder associated with abnormal defecation and mucosal prolapse. Its clinical and endoscopic features may mimic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We report the case of a 28-year-old woman with longstanding obstructed defecation who presented with recurrent bloody mucus discharge and severe iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL), which was treated with intravenous iron infusions. C-reactive protein was normal, whereas fecal calprotectin was markedly elevated. Initial colonoscopy showed erythematous and congested mucosa extending from the anal verge to 20 cm, with a large ulcer, raising suspicion of ulcerative colitis. However, the initial biopsies were inconclusive. Following clinical worsening, repeat colonoscopy revealed a 5-cm elevated rectal lesion with central ulceration. Histological examination demonstrated epithelial loss, granulation tissue, villiform crypt changes, and characteristic fibromuscular hyperplasia of the lamina propria, establishing the diagnosis of SRUS. Magnetic resonance defecography revealed an anterior rectocele and internal rectal prolapse, while anorectal manometry demonstrated dyssynergic defecation. Conservative measures and biofeedback provided incomplete improvement, with persistent rectal bleeding. Given the documented internal rectal prolapse and refractory symptoms, laparoscopic ventral rectopexy was performed, resulting in a favorable postoperative clinical course with marked symptomatic improvement and normalization of hemoglobin to 13.7 g/dL. SRUS should be considered when inflammatory-appearing rectal lesions are not supported by histological evidence of IBD, particularly in patients with obstructed defecation.

title: A Volumetric Anatomy-Aware, Prompt-Guided Adaptation Framework for the Segment Anything Model in Head and Neck Radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Head and neck (H&N) radiotherapy planning requires accurate segmentation of numerous organs at risk (OARs), yet many critical structures, such as the optic nerves, chiasm, and cochleae, are small, poorly contrasted on CT, and prone to high inter-observer variability in manual contouring. Recent foundation models like Segment Anything Model (SAM) and its 3D medical variants (SAM-Med3D) offer prompt-based, interactive segmentation, but their real-world utility for H&N small OARs is hindered by unreliable prompt sources and unstable performance on fine anatomical targets. To address these issues, this work proposes an anatomy-aware prompt generation and prompt-guided adaptation tailored specifically for small-structure segmentation to improve both precision and automation feasibility. Purpose To address these challenges, we developed a domain-adapted framework, SAM-FT-HN, by fine-tuning a volumetric SAM backbone (SAM-Med3D) for automated delineation of H&N OARs in radiotherapy planning. Our approach incorporates a coarse-to-fine pipeline in which a lightweight localization network automatically generates organ-specific prompts and candidate regions, followed by a fine-tuned volumetric SAM backbone for refinement. We further introduced task-specific strategies including region-of-interest (ROI)-guided tiny-organ enhancement and organ-specific threshold calibration to improve performance on small structures. The primary objective is to develop and evaluate a fully automated, anatomy-aware adaptation of SAM-Med3D for H&N OAR segmentation, with a secondary objective of improving small-organ segmentation. We systematically compared SAM-FT-HN against baseline SAM-Med3D and nnUNet models quantitatively and qualitatively. Methods We used an institutional H&N CT dataset of 211 patients with manual delineations of 23 OARs, standardized for training, validation, and testing. Eighty percent of cases were used for training and validation, and twenty percent for testing. The testing phase used CT volumes only, and ground-truth masks were used solely for metric calculation. A coarse localization network was trained to generate automatic prompts and ROI candidates. SAM-FT-HN was fine-tuned using task-specific adaptations, and small-organ refinement was performed using ROI-guided enhancement and organ-specific threshold calibration. nnUNet was trained using its automated configuration pipeline. Performance was evaluated using overlap and boundary metrics. Results For large OARs, SAM-FT-HN achieved a mean Dice of 0.814 compared with 0.791 for nnUNet and substantially higher than SAM-Med3D (0.609). For small organs, SAM-FT-HN improved the mean Dice from 0.300 to 0.669 compared with SAM-Med3D and reduced HD95 by approximately 65%, although nnUNet remained higher in average small-organ Dice (0.720). Overall, across all organs, SAM-FT-HN achieved a mean Dice score of 0.770, compared with 0.769 for nnUNet. Overall, SAM-FT-HN showed no statistically significant difference from nnUNet in the patient-level analysis, while substantially outperforming the original SAM-Med3D baseline. Conclusion Fine-tuning a foundation model with anatomy-aware automatic prompting, coarse-to-fine localization, and adaptive thresholding markedly improves small-organ segmentation, substantially mitigating a key limitation of the original foundation model. SAM-FT-HN offers a competitive approach for H&N radiotherapy contouring, with potential for future adaptive workflows.

title: Multilevel Lumbar Epidural Angiolipoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Spinal angiolipomas are rare benign tumors composed of mature adipose tissue and vascular elements, most commonly located in the thoracic epidural space. Lumbar involvement is considerably less frequent, and variable proportions of adipose and vascular tissue may result in atypical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics and diagnostic uncertainty. We report the case of a 36-year-old woman with an approximately one-year history of persistent low back pain associated with subjective bilateral lower-extremity weakness despite a preserved neurological examination. An initial non-contrast lumbar MRI was interpreted as showing no significant abnormality other than minimal degenerative changes; however, retrospective review revealed a subtle posterior epidural lesion. Because of persistent symptoms, further investigation with contrast-enhanced MRI was performed, demonstrating an elongated epidural lesion extending from L1 to L3, predominantly involving the posterior and right posterolateral epidural space with associated foraminal extension. The lesion demonstrated areas of low T1 signal intensity and intense homogeneous contrast enhancement. The patient underwent L1-L3 laminoplasty and gross-total resection. Intraoperatively, the lesion had a macroscopically adipose appearance and was moderately vascular. Histopathological examination demonstrated mature adipose tissue admixed with numerous vascular channels, confirming the diagnosis of spinal angiolipoma. Postoperatively, pain and subjective lower-extremity weakness improved without new neurological deficits, and early postoperative MRI showed no evidence of residual or recurrent tumor. This case highlights the variable imaging appearance of lumbar spinal angiolipomas and the value of correlating MRI characteristics with intraoperative and histopathological findings, particularly in enhancing epidural lesions without a predominantly fatty appearance.

title: Fever and Painful Skin Lesions: When to Consider Sweet's Syndrome.
abstract: Sweet's syndrome is an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis characterised by fever, neutrophilia, and painful cutaneous lesions. We describe a case of a 31-year-old male admitted with a two-week history of fever up to 39°C and painful erythematous papules, scattered and coalescing into plaques over the trunk and limbs, together with pustules on an erythematous base over the palms and dorsum of the hands. No relevant epidemiological exposure or recent drug exposure was identified. Investigation showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h, leucocytosis of 14,380/µL with 77% neutrophils and no eosinophilia, and a C-reactive protein of 1.21 mg/dL. Liver and renal function, albumin, lactate dehydrogenase, serum iron, ferritin, and serum protein electrophoresis were normal, and a respiratory viral panel was negative. Blood, urine, and pustule cultures, an interferon-gamma release assay, and serology for human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, hepatitis A, B, C, and E viruses, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus were negative, as was an autoantibody panel. Serum immunoglobulin A was below the detection limit (<0.07 g/L) before corticosteroid therapy and on all repeat measurements, including after treatment had been discontinued, with normal immunoglobulin G and M, and IgG-based coeliac serology was negative. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed no abnormalities. A skin biopsy demonstrated intraepidermal blisters and a superficial perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis, spongiform pustules, or psoriasiform changes. The clinical and laboratory criteria for classical Sweet's syndrome were fulfilled, and the histology was compatible with, although not classical for, the syndrome. Prednisolone 60 mg/day (approximately 0.6 mg/kg/day) was started on clinical suspicion of the syndrome. After one week, the fever had resolved, but the lesions worsened slightly, prompting escalation to 100 mg/day (approximately 1 mg/kg/day), after which they regressed progressively and resolved completely within three weeks of dose escalation, with normalisation of the leucocyte count. Corticosteroids were tapered and discontinued before the three-month assessment, at which there was no relapse and no evidence of malignancy. This case illustrates three practical points: an acral pustular morphology does not exclude the diagnosis; early worsening under corticosteroid therapy may reflect an initial dose insufficient for body weight rather than an incorrect diagnosis, once infection has been rigorously excluded; and the coexisting finding of selective immunoglobulin A deficiency carries independent implications for coeliac disease screening and long-term follow-up.

title: Managing Severe Proximal Femoral Fibrous Dysplasia in a Young Adult Using Hemiarthroplasty in a Resource-Constrained Healthcare System: A Case Report.
abstract: Fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur may lead to progressive deformity, pain, and pathological fractures, with shepherd's crook deformity representing one of its most severe manifestations. Although valgus osteotomy with intramedullary fixation is considered the preferred surgical treatment, extensive bone destruction and limited healthcare resources may preclude conventional reconstruction. We present a case of severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia successfully managed with bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty in a resource-constrained healthcare setting. A 25-year-old man presented with progressive left hip pain, severe proximal femoral deformity, and impaired ambulation. Radiographic evaluation demonstrated lateral bowing of the proximal femur, while histopathological examination following core biopsy confirmed fibrous dysplasia. Internal fixation using an intramedullary nail was initially planned; however, intraoperative findings revealed extensive fibro-osseous replacement, severely compromised bone quality, and inadequate cortical support, making stable fixation technically impossible. Because more complex reconstructive procedures were not covered by the national health insurance system, a bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty, augmented with plate fixation of the osteotomized fragments, was performed as a salvage procedure. The postoperative course was uneventful, with marked pain relief, improved gait, and satisfactory functional recovery at 10 months of follow-up (Oxford Hip Score 34/48). Conventional fixation for shepherd's crook deformity requires adequate residual cortical bone to achieve stable implant fixation. In cases with extensive cortical destruction and bone stock too thin to support reliable press-fit fixation, cemented hemiarthroplasty may represent a practical alternative. Preservation of the native acetabulum may also reduce postoperative instability while providing satisfactory functional outcomes. Bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty may be an effective salvage option for selected patients with severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia when conventional fixation is technically unfeasible, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare systems.

title: Phyllodes Tumors of the Breast in 2026: A Contemporary Narrative Review of Diagnosis, Surgical Margins, Prognosis, and Emerging Therapies.
abstract: Phyllodes tumors of the breast are rare fibroepithelial neoplasms characterized by significant heterogeneity regarding morphology, biological behavior, and clinical outcome. This review summarizes current developments in the diagnosis, histopathological and molecular classification, therapeutic management, and emerging technologies associated with phyllodes tumors of the breast. A literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and Google Scholar, focusing on publications from the 2000-2026 period. The literature search covered publications from January 1, 2000, to September 30, 2026, and was last updated on September 30, 2026. Mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging contribute to preoperative assessment, although significant diagnostic overlap with fibroadenomas persists. Core needle biopsy is a key diagnostic tool, yet lesion heterogeneity can limit the accuracy of histological classification. Advances in molecular pathology have identified mutations and pathways associated with the progression and aggressiveness of phyllodes tumors, though these have not yet replaced morphological assessment. Surgical excision with negative margins remains the primary therapeutic approach, while the risk of local recurrence depends on histological grade, surgical margins, and other clinicopathological characteristics. Radiotherapy in phyllodes tumors of the breast appears to offer benefits primarily regarding local control in selected high-risk cases. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, radiomics, and digital pathology, are proving to be promising tools for diagnosis, grading, and prognostic assessment. Overall, modern management of phyllodes tumors of the breast is shifting toward more personalized and multifactorial approaches.

title: When Appearances Deceive: A Silent Somatotroph Macroadenoma Presenting With Acromegaloid Features and Paradoxically Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1.
abstract: Silent somatotroph adenomas are uncommon pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs) of the PIT1 lineage that express growth hormone (GH) immunohistochemically but without biochemical evidence of acromegaly. We report the case of a 32-year-old male patient referred with recurrent epistaxis, headache, right-sided diplopia, and third cranial nerve palsy. Clinical examination revealed acromegaloid features including frontal bossing, spade-like hands, and coarse facies, which were strongly suggestive of longstanding GH excess. However, preoperative insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) was paradoxically low at 13.1 nmol/L (reference range 15.5-33.1 nmol/L), creating a striking clinical-biochemical discordance. MRI demonstrated a giant sellar and suprasellar mass with chiasmal compression, right cavernous sinus invasion, and extension into the paranasal sinuses. The patient underwent endoscopic transsphenoidal resection. Neuropathology confirmed a densely granulated PIT1-lineage somatotroph adenoma with scattered GH positivity, diffuse Pit-1 staining, and a Ki-67 index below 2%. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by silent somatotroph adenomas, underscores the limitations of biochemical assessment alone, and reinforces the essential role of histopathology and immunohistochemistry in establishing a definitive diagnosis. Long-term endocrine and neurosurgical surveillance is strongly recommended given the potential for phenotypic transformation to a functioning acromegaly syndrome.

title: Ovarian Myxoma in a Patient With Missed Abortion: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
abstract: Ovarian myxoma is a rare benign mesenchymal tumor. It can be completely asymptomatic and is difficult to differentiate from other ovarian masses before surgery and final histopathology. We report a case of a 28-year-old primigravida who presented with a missed abortion at 11 weeks. Transvaginal ultrasonography incidentally showed a 6.5 × 5.7 cm complex solid-cystic right adnexal lesion in the pouch of Douglas. She was asymptomatic from the mass. After dilatation and evacuation for missed abortion, the patient was evaluated for an ovarian mass, and tumor markers were found negative. Repeat ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous lesion with coarse hyperechoic foci and posterior acoustic shadowing, suggesting a right ovarian teratoma. The patient was taken for laparotomy, wherein an 8 × 8 cm solid-cystic mass was found in the right ovary, and right ovarian cystectomy was done. Intraoperative scrape cytology came back negative for malignancy and showed columnar cells, squamous cells, and mature adipose tissue, which favored a benign cystic teratoma. Histopathology showed a thick collagenous capsule and stellate cells in abundant myxoid stroma without atypia. On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were positive for vimentin and negative for desmin and cytokeratin. The final diagnosis was ovarian myxoma. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. There was no recurrence at one-year follow-up. This case shows that ovarian myxoma can mimic a mature cystic teratoma on imaging, gross examination, and cytology, and that the final diagnosis depends on histopathological examination (HPE) supported by immunohistochemistry.

title: Diffuse-Type Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Flexor Hallucis Longus Tendon Sheath: A Case Report.
abstract: The synovium can be the primary site for the development of various benign or malignant tumors. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), also known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, is a benign but locally aggressive synovial neoplasm occurring in localized and diffuse forms. The localized form predominantly affects the hand, whereas the diffuse form mainly involves large joints; involvement of the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath is rare. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the principal modality for demonstrating the hemosiderin deposits characteristic of this lesion, although histopathology remains necessary for definitive diagnosis. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment. We report the case of a 24-year-old man with 10 months of right ankle pain, related to a diffuse-type TGCT involving the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath and adjacent ankle joints. Radiographs initially showed soft-tissue filling of Kager's triangle. Computed tomography arthrography demonstrated synovial thickening but was nonspecific; MRI then revealed the characteristic findings, and histopathology confirmed the diagnosis. This report aims to raise awareness of this rare location and its associated diagnostic pitfalls.

title: Congenital Hypoplasia of the C1 Posterior Arch Masquerading as Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Report.
abstract: Hypoplasia of the C1 posterior arch is a rare congenital anomaly, classified using the Currarino system into subtypes A through E depending on the extent and nature of arch deficiency. The majority of cases are incidental radiological findings; symptomatic presentations causing cervical myelopathy are exceptionally uncommon and not well represented in the surgical literature. In such cases, the absence of established management guidelines renders clinical decision-making particularly challenging. We present a case of a 45-year-old male surgeon who presented with a one-year history of episodic bilateral upper and lower limb weakness. Initial investigations, including brain and cervical spine MRI, were interpreted as consistent with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, for which treatment was commenced. Following a symptom-free interval after a one-month course of corticosteroids, the patient experienced a recurrence at eight months, prompting dynamic MRI of the cervical spine, which revealed a type C hypoplastic C1 posterior arch causing dynamic spinal cord compression during hyperextension. The diagnosis was revised accordingly. Supplementary investigations confirmed atlantoaxial stability and normal vertebral artery anatomy bilaterally. The patient provided consent and underwent posterior surgical decompression of the entire posterior arch, without instrumented fusion. Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring guided the extent of resection; decompression began on the fibrous left-sided arch, extending to the level of the vertebral artery groove, followed by the bony right-sided arch, sequenced to preserve facet joint integrity. The patient achieved complete symptom resolution postoperatively. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by symptomatic C1 arch hypoplasia, which may mimic demyelinating disease, and demonstrates that surgical decompression, guided by intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring and tailored to arch morphology, can achieve excellent neurological outcomes without the need for instrumented stabilisation.

Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring guided the extent of resection; decompression began on the fibrous left-sided arch, extending to the level of the vertebral artery groove, followed by the bony right-sided arch, sequenced to preserve facet joint integrity. The patient achieved complete symptom resolution postoperatively. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by symptomatic C1 arch hypoplasia, which may mimic demyelinating disease, and demonstrates that surgical decompression, guided by intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring and tailored to arch morphology, can achieve excellent neurological outcomes without the need for instrumented stabilisation.

title: Diagnostic Tools Used for Tuberculous Pleural Effusion and Their Association With Treatment Outcomes.
abstract: Background Tuberculous pleural effusion (TPE) is difficult to confirm because pleural disease is often paucibacillary. Pleural-fluid biomarkers, culture, molecular assays, and pleural biopsy can improve diagnostic certainty, but their availability varies substantially in resource-limited settings. Objective To describe the diagnostic investigations used for suspected TPE at AlShaab and Abu Anjaa Teaching Hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan, from February to July 2017, and assess their association with treatment outcomes. Methodology This retrospective cohort study included 69 patients with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of TPE at two teaching hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan, from February to July 2017. The first author collected demographic, clinical, investigation, treatment, and outcome data from patient records using a standardized data-collection checklist. Investigations were classified according to whether a test and result were documented. Associations with outcome were assessed using Fisher's exact test and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Chest radiography was performed in 67/69 patients (97.1%). Pleural-fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) was recorded in 1/69 (1.4%), culture in 6/69 (8.7%), polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 4/69 (5.8%), and pleural biopsy in 7/69 (10.1%). GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA) and pleural-fluid interferon-gamma testing were not performed. HIV testing was not documented in 50/69 patients (72.5%). Thirteen patients (18.8%) received antituberculous treatment without pleural-fluid or tissue testing. Five (38.5%) had a favorable outcome, and eight (61.5%) had an unfavorable outcome, including four subsequently diagnosed with malignant effusion and one death. Among 56 patients who underwent at least one pleural-fluid or tissue test, 39 (69.6%) had a favorable outcome. Any diagnostic testing was associated with higher odds of favorable outcome (OR 3.67, 95% CI 1.05-12.87; Fisher's exact P = 0.054), although the association did not cross the conventional statistical-significance threshold. Conclusions Confirmatory testing for suspected TPE was used inconsistently, while several clinically useful tests were rarely or never available. Patients treated without pleural-fluid or tissue testing had more unfavorable outcomes, including missed malignant effusion. The findings support a pragmatic minimum diagnostic bundle before prolonged empiric treatment, while recognizing that this observational study cannot establish that testing caused better outcomes.

title: A Case of Advanced Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck: Diagnostic Challenges and Sequential Systemic Therapy.
abstract: Advanced cutaneous malignancies with basaloid morphology can present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, particularly when pathological interpretations differ and disease progresses during systemic treatment. We describe the clinical course of a 53-year-old woman with an extensive, unresectable cutaneous tumor involving the posterior neck and occipital region, accompanied by bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and additional clinically suspected cutaneous deposits. The initial diagnosis was trichoblastic carcinoma, whereas expert pathological review favored basal cell carcinoma. The extent of disease precluded surgery and definitive radiotherapy. First-line vismodegib was initiated, and palliative radiotherapy delivering 30 Gy in 10 fractions to the occipital lesions and bilateral cervical lymph nodes was completed one year later. Clinical progression was documented three months after completion of radiotherapy; one month after this, MRI demonstrated extensive infiltration involving the left parotid gland and adjacent pharyngeal spaces. Second-line cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil were subsequently administered. Follow-up MRI six months after the earlier MRI demonstrated substantial tumor volume reduction. PET/CT three months later showed a heterogeneous response compared with a year earlier, including regression at several previously involved sites and newly apparent metabolically active right axillary lymph nodes. A subsequent biopsy was reported as basaloid carcinoma. The patient later experienced clinical deterioration, received one cycle of cemiplimab, and died before further treatment or response assessment. This case illustrates the importance of pathological clarification, longitudinal imaging, and careful interpretation of treatment response during sequential systemic therapy for advanced basal cell carcinoma.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Computed Tomography for Radiographically Occult Scaphoid Fractures and Concordance With Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fracture. Non-union and avascular necrosis are complications of a missed fracture. Therefore, if plain radiographs are normal and symptoms persist, further imaging such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often performed. Previous systematic reviews have largely compared their diagnostic accuracy indirectly using separate patient cohorts. Our objective is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of CT for occult scaphoid fractures in patients who underwent both CT and MRI following a negative or equivocal initial radiograph, and to assess concordance between CT and MRI findings. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. OVID MEDLINE, OVID Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from inception up to August 31, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled adults with clinically suspected scaphoid fracture and a negative or equivocal initial radiograph who subsequently underwent both CT and MRI. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2). Studies affected by partial verification or incorporation bias were excluded from quantitative synthesis. CT sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. Concordance between CT and MRI was reported using percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Six studies contributed to the primary pooled analysis of CT diagnostic accuracy, with one study reporting two CT readers. Using the first reader data from that study, alongside the five other studies, pooled CT sensitivity was 79% (95% CI 61.5-89.8%) and specificity was 94.4% (95% CI 82.1-98.4%). A sensitivity analysis using the second reader produced a sensitivity of 69.2% (95% CI 48.0-84.6%), with an unchanged specificity of 94.4% (95% CI 85.5-98.0%). Three studies provided CT-MRI concordance data; two demonstrated almost perfect agreement, with Cohen's kappa values of 0.91. The dual-energy CT study demonstrated lower concordance. Three studies used a reference standard independent of both CT and MRI and demonstrated mixed comparative findings. Overall, one study was judged to have low risk of bias, and seven were high risk of bias. In the included studies, CT demonstrated high specificity but more limited sensitivity for occult scaphoid fracture in paired CT-MRI cohorts. These findings align with existing literature reviewing unpaired data sets. Therefore, the findings suggest that CT remains a relevant alternative to MRI, especially in centres where MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, or for surgical planning.

title: Rapidly Evolving Aphasia as a Diagnostic Clue in First-Episode Psychosis: A Case Report of Anti-NMDAR Encephalitis.
abstract: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis frequently presents with isolated psychiatric symptoms indistinguishable from primary psychosis, delaying diagnosis. The authors have described a previously healthy 35-year-old woman admitted with abrupt first-episode psychosis, who (within 48 hours and without seizures, movement disorder, or altered consciousness) developed a true aphasic syndrome, fluctuating output with semantic and phonemic paraphasias and intermittent mutism, distinct from the disorganized speech of primary psychosis. The emergence of focal language disturbance prompted neurologic evaluation. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable; cerebrospinal fluid showed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and a raised immunoglobulin G index, with anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor immunoglobulin G strongly positive in cerebrospinal fluid. Pelvic imaging identified an ovarian teratoma, which was resected. First-line immunotherapy (intravenous methylprednisolone and immunoglobulin) followed by plasma exchange, with short-term antipsychotic treatment, achieved sustained remission. Serial neuropsychological assessment over 18 months documented a heterogeneous recovery trajectory: early, near-complete recovery of graphomotor speed and verbal consolidation, slower recovery of associative and working-memory functions, and verbal working memory persisting as the most stable residual deficit. This case showed that rapidly evolving aphasia, distinguished at the bedside from schizophasia, can localize an autoimmune process beyond any primary psychiatric differential and trigger the workup that secures the diagnosis.

title: Cystic Fibrosis
abstract: Clinical characteristics Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem disease affecting epithelia of the respiratory tract, pancreas, intestine, hepatobiliary system, and exocrine sweat glands. Morbidities include progressive obstructive pulmonary disease with bronchiectasis, recurrent sinusitis and bronchitis, exocrine pancreatic deficiency and malnutrition, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal manifestations (meconium ileus, rectal prolapse, distal intestinal obstructive syndrome), liver disease, diabetes, osteopenia/osteoporosis, male infertility due to hypoplasia or aplasia of the vas deferens, and reduced fertility or infertility in some women. By 2025, 95% of individuals with CF were eligible for targeted therapies, which has significantly altered the long-term course of the disease with a reduced overall disease burden. The impact is most evident in fewer hospitalizations, reduced clinic visits, and a decreased need for lung transplantation, all of which are associated with improved survival. While the CF disease phenotype has overall become less severe and more heterogenous in the era of highly effective CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy, pulmonary disease is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in CF. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of CF is established in a proband with (1) elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening, signs and/or symptoms suggestive of CF, or family history of CF; AND (2) evidence of an abnormality in CFTR function: sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L on sweat chloride testing, biallelic CFTR CF-causing pathogenic variants, or nasal transmembrane epithelial potential difference measurement consistent with CF. Management Targeted therapies: CFTR modulator therapy is available for individuals with responsive CFTR variants. These should be prescribed and managed by a clinician with CF expertise, particularly when initiating therapy. Supportive care: Newborns – management by a CF specialist or CF care center; airway clearance instruction; encouraging feeding with breast milk; routine vaccinations; contact precautions with every clinical encounter; antibiotics for bacterial suppression and treatment; nutrition management; pancreatic enzyme replacement; nutrient-dense food and supplements; fat-soluble vitamin supplements; laxative treatment as needed with surgical management for bowel obstruction; salt supplementation as needed. After the newborn period – airway clearance; pulmonary treatment (bronchodilator, hypertonic saline, dornase alfa, airway clearance, and aerosolized antibiotic); standard treatments for pneumothorax or hemoptysis; double lung transplant for those with advanced lung disease; routine vaccinations including influenza; contact precautions; antibiotics for bacterial suppression and treatment; antibiotics and/or surgical intervention for nasal/sinus symptoms; nutrition management; pancreatic enzyme replacement; nutrient-dense food and supplements; fat-soluble vitamin supplements; laxative treatment as needed with surgical management for bowel obstruction; standard treatments for gastroesophageal reflux disease; liver transplant when indicated; management of CF-related diabetes mellitus by an endocrinologist; assisted reproductive technologies (ART) for infertility; salt supplementation; standard treatments for associated mental health issues. Surveillance: Frequent assessment by a CF specialist to monitor for new or worsening manifestations; pulmonary function testing frequently after age five years; consider chest CT to assess for bronchiectasis every two years or as needed; cultures of respiratory tract secretions at least every three months; non-tuberculosis mycobacterium culture and measurement of serum immunoglobulin E annually or as indicated; annual complete blood count with differential; ENT assessment as needed; monitor growth and gastrointestinal manifestations at each visit; fecal elastase as needed; annual serum vitamin A, D, E, and prothrombin time (as a marker of vitamin K); colon cancer screening at least every five years beginning at age 40 years (beginning at age 30 years in transplant recipients); annual liver function tests; liver ultrasound with Doppler every two years starting at age three years; annual measurement of random blood glucose; annual two-hour glucose tolerance test beginning at age ten years; dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan in adolescence in those with risk factors for osteopenia, then every one to five years; infertility assessment as needed; annual electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine; annual assessment for depression and anxiety. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Environmental smoke and inhalants including electronic nicotine delivery products, exposure to respiratory infections, and dehydration. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Sweat chloride testing is recommended for all at-risk sibs of a proband to identify as early as possible those who should be referred to a CF center for initiation of early treatment. Genetic counseling CF is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a CFTR pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being heterozygous, and a 25% chance of inheriting neither of the familial pathogenic variants. Heterozygotes may be at increased risk for respiratory manifestations and/or pancreatitis. Once the CFTR pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, targeted heterozygote testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing for CF are possible.
